s: Tonight our subject is one of the two young men we read about in Luke chapter 15.
Every person here tonight knows Luke chapter 15 just as well as the preacher does.
There is probably not a prodigal in all of New York who doesn’t know the story told in this chapter of Luke.
I don’t need to tell you why this young man went away.
It was his nature.
It is natural for a person to go away from God.
“We have all gone astray like sheep.” Every one of us turns away far too easily.
This prodigal left without any reason that we know of. We are not told that his father was unkind to him. But I do think the father made a mistake.
Suppose I had a son who wanted me to divide up my property and give him his share. I think it would be a big mistake to give him the money.
A lot of people are making that mistake today. If anyone in this world deserves pity more than others, it is the man who has all the money he wants to spend and nothing to do.
When that young man came to his father and asked for his share, his father should have said, “No, you should wait until your father is gone.”
When the prodigal son got what was coming to him, the story says he gathered all his things together and traveled to a distant country.

In that distant country people thought he was popular. Most men who have plenty of money and nothing to do are very popular. But we are not told how long his popularity lasted, because we don’t know exactly how long his money lasted.

His friends gathered around him. He had many friends until his money was gone. Then the poor man woke up to the truth: all those he called his friends had been after his money, not him. They were friends of his money, not friends of his.
And when he had spent everything, he finally ended up in need.
Have you ever stopped to think how many prodigals there are in a city like New York?
Suppose we had them all here tonight and could let them walk past in front of this audience. It would take a long, long time—tramp, tramp, tramp—for them all to pass in front of this crowd.
New York is full of prodigals.
They have not only left their parents here on earth. They have sent many of those parents to an early grave.
And how many have turned their backs on God and wandered away!
I don’t know where the prodigal son in this story went. Perhaps to Egypt. Perhaps he went to Memphis, which was one of the splendid cities in those days. But he got as far away from home as he could.
Maybe he wanted to get away from the rules and influences of home. Maybe he talked the way many young men do now, laughing and saying he was only “sowing his wild oats.”
It makes my heart sad when I hear young men say that.
Many young men seem to forget that they will have to reap ten times what they sow.
If a man plants a handful, he harvests a bushel. If a man sows the wind, he reaps the whirlwind. It is only a matter of time. Some day he will surely end up in need.
All these earthly streams run dry some day. He will surely end up in need.
We read that when this prodigal’s money was all gone, a famine struck that land. There he was, alone in a foreign country, in great need.
All his friends were gone now. He had lost every one of them. He thought he had many friends, but now they were all gone.
If they had had pawnshops in those days, you would have seen him hanging around a pawnshop, pawning whatever he had left.
The rings he wore when he left home are gone. Maybe he has worn out his shoes, so he can’t even pawn them. There he is, stripped of everything.
But he didn’t go and beg, like so many men do these days.
I respect the prodigal for that one thing: he did go to work.

It was a very humble job, of course. But if he couldn’t get what he wanted, he was willing to do almost anything rather than beg. For a Jew there is no lower job than feeding pigs, but he was willing to do it.
If many of the people we now call tramps would go to work, we would all feel sympathy for them.
The prodigal sank very low, but not so low that he would beg. He went to work. His work was very lowly. He could not have had a lower job than feeding those pigs.
When a backslider goes away from God, he loses all the blessing of his work. And the prodigal lost all of his.
He had no home.
A man who is away from God has no home. He has turned his back on his home, and there was no home for him there among strangers.
Even if the strangers had tried to give him a home, it would not have been home to him. But they didn’t.

There he was among strangers, with no coat, no shoes, and no hat. Some of the young men of that country came by. Perhaps some of them were the very friends who had taken his money from him, for men gambled back then just as they do now. They probably said, “Look at that fool! He came down here with $20,000 only two or three years ago, and now he has wasted it all.”
The very men who had taken his money now began to make fun of him.
I can almost see him standing up straight and saying to them, “You call me a beggar!
Why, my father’s servants dress better than you do!”
They laughed and said, “Your father’s servants? Why, you don’t even have a father.”
No one believed him. He had lost his testimony.
In the same way, every backslider who has turned away from God has lost his testimony.
You can never find food for your soul in the devil’s country.
There he was, far from home and starving. No one would give him even the food the pigs ate.
He wished he could fill his belly with the husks the pigs were eating.
Sin had taken him away from home and away from God. The question is, how did he ever get back?
I suppose all you prodigals want to know how he got back. You want to know how to get back yourselves—hundreds of you here tonight.
When the man began to come to his senses, he realized that the best friend he had in the world was his father.
There was one thing the prodigal never lost. He lost his work, his food, his home, and his testimony. But he never lost his father’s love.
His father kept on loving him through it all.
I find that many men who are living in sin wonder why God doesn’t answer their prayers.
Well, God loves them too much to answer their prayers.
Suppose the son had written his father a letter saying, “I’m in need. Why don’t you send me some money?”
The father would have loved him too much to answer that prayer.
Your Father in heaven loves you too much.
Maybe you have gone off into a foreign country, away from God’s table. If so, His arms will not reach you there to feed you and clothe you.
He wants you to go home to Him.
That man had left home and gone to a foreign land, and the famine was hitting him hard.
One day a neighbor came down, perhaps from his home country, and found the young man there.
He said, “Why don’t you go home?”
“Well, I don’t know.
I’m not sure my father will take me back.”
“Your father? He loves you as much as he ever did.”
“My father? Did you see him?”
“Yes, I was talking with your father one day last week.”
“What did he say?
Does he ever talk about me?”
“Ever talk about you!
He never talks about anyone else.
He dreams about you at night.”
Oh, if there is a poor prodigal here tonight, don’t keep believing the terrible, false idea that your father has forgotten you.
Think of a father who has nine children. One of them is a prodigal, away from home. Yet he thinks more about that one son than about all the rest.
One of the biggest obstacles a man has is his terrible pride.
This young man says, “I left with plenty.
I left in grand style, and now I have to go back in rags.”
Maybe his pride kept him away for a while.
One day he came to his senses and decided to go back to his father’s house.
He got down on his knees and buried his face in his hands, like Elijah on Mount Carmel, and he began to think.
He was deep in thought, and he says, “Well, maybe I had better go home.
I think perhaps I should.

In fact, no one in the world loves me as much as my father.” Then he lets his mind go back into the past. It sweeps over his whole life, all the way back to his childhood. He remembers his father and mother—how they loved him and how they watched over him.
He thinks of his mother’s tears.
I can’t help thinking that his mother had died. No one could care more about the boy than his mother, and the story doesn’t say anything about her.
He thinks about how, after mother died, father was almost as tender as mother.
He says, “I remember the morning I left home. The old man wept and sobbed over me.

He tried to hide his feelings, but I remember how he begged me to stay home. I remember how he prayed that morning at the family altar. He asked the Lord God of heaven to save his boy from sin, and he asked God to send His angels to watch over me.”
He was miles away, but everything back in his hometown was vivid in his mind.
He says, “Here I am with no shoes and no coat, covered in nothing but these miserable rags.”
He looked ahead into the future, and it looked so dark.
“Why, even the servants are better off than I am! There is more than enough bread in my father’s house.” And the young man came to his senses and said, “I will.”
That is when his heart turned back to his God.
I pray to God that thousands would say those words tonight: “I will get up and go to my Father.”
Nine-tenths of the battle was won when he said, “I will get up and go to my father.”
He may be in a far country, but he will soon get home if he has made up his mind to come.
And he put together a kind of sermon that he planned to preach when he got home.
The first thing he planned to do was confess.
“I will confess that I have sinned against heaven.
I will confess that I have done wrong, and I will ask him to let me be one of his servants.”
Ah, he didn’t know his father’s heart! If he had, he wouldn’t have asked for the rest.
He says, “I will just ask my father to let me be one of his servants.”
But now he had made up his mind to go home, and he sets out.
He goes to the citizen of that country and says, “I have decided to go home. I can’t work for you anymore.
My father is well off, and I’m sure my father will take me back.”
The citizen doesn’t care about him at all. But back home there is a living heart, and he sets out.
I see him on his way, and now there is joy up there. They ring the bells of heaven.
I see the guardian angel who watches over him. The moment he came to his senses, there was joy in heaven.
Then the prodigal is on his way—look at him!
I can just imagine how he felt as he crossed the border of his homeland: “Maybe father has died. Maybe he is dead?
If he is, maybe I won’t get a warm welcome.”
It was a good thing for the prodigal that his father was alive, wasn’t it?
He wouldn’t have gotten a very warm welcome from that brother of his.
Ah, young man, you had better learn from that experience. Get home before your old father dies—unless you have a godly, praying mother.
Go home tonight and write a letter to your mother or your father, and ask them to forgive you!
Ask your Father in heaven to forgive you.
But now look at him as he walks toward home, wondering if his father is alive and waiting for him.
There is the old man out on the flat roof.
He has been up there many times before.
Many times he has looked in the direction his boy went.
He can’t recognize him by his clothes, but love has sharp eyes.
He saw his boy far away. It was his long-lost boy!
He sets off toward him.
You can see his long white hair flying in the air. He leaps along the road. He feels young again.
The servants watch him leaping along the road, and they wonder what has come over him.
This is the only time God is pictured as running—just to meet a poor sinner.
God walks. When the children of Israel were thrown into the fiery furnace, we see that God walked in that furnace.
The whole story of the prodigal was written just to show God’s love, the compassion of God.
“And when he saw him a long way off, he felt compassion for him.”
He didn’t wait for him to arrive.
He didn’t say, “He left for no reason. I won’t go out to meet him.”
When he reaches him, he throws his arms around his neck and weeps over him. The servants come running out to see what is going on.
The boy begins his speech: “Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am not worthy anymore to be called your son!”

Just as he was about to say, “Make me one of your hired servants,” the father interrupts him. He says to one servant, “Go and bring the best robe and put it on him.” To another he says, “Go to my jewelry box, get a ring, and put it on his finger.” To another, “Go and get the shoes.” And to another, “Go and kill the fattened calf.”
And there was joy there.
What joy there was in that home!
“He felt compassion for him.”

My friend, don’t you know that ever since then this story has been repeated almost every day? Prodigals are going back. And I have never yet heard of any man going back who did not get a warm welcome.
There isn’t a poor prodigal in New York who won’t get a warm welcome if he goes back to his father.
But that isn’t the lesson we want to teach.
My friends, it is not only about making peace with your earthly father, but with your Father in heaven.
The most sensible thing you can do is go to your Father in heaven and ask Him to forgive you.
I have a letter here. I think it is one of the last letters I received from England.

The letter says that a son and husband had left his father’s house. He had left his wife and children for no reason. Now, at the end of the letter, his sister says, “He doesn’t need to fear any blame. Only love is waiting for him at home.”
That man may be here tonight.
My words may reach him. If so, I beg him to turn back from his wrong ways.
Listen! Your sister says that no blame or harsh words will meet you when you come home. Only love will welcome you when you walk through the door.
Oh, don’t reject your sister’s words, or the tears of your loved ones far away.
The prodigal’s father did not blame his boy. He had no unkind words for him when he came back from his wanderings.
And in the same way, God does not blame the sinner.
He knows what human nature is like—how easily a person goes astray.
It is human to make mistakes.
He is always ready to forgive you and take you back.
Christ says He will forgive. He is full of love, compassion, and tenderness.
If a poor sinner comes and confesses, God is willing and ready to forgive you.
He will forgive you the very hour—yes, the very minute—you come back.
Oh, you who have gone astray, remember this.
A lady once came to Liverpool to see us privately. It was just before we were going to leave that city to go to London to preach.
Crying and sobbing, she told a very sad story.
This was it: she said she had a nineteen-year-old son who had left her.
She showed me his photograph and asked me to put it in my pocket.
“You stand before many large crowds, Mr. Moody.
My boy may be in London now.
Oh, look at the crowds you will preach to. Look carefully.
You may see my dear boy in front of you.
If you do see him, tell him to come back to me.
Oh, beg him to come back to his grieving mother and to the home he has left.
He may be in trouble. He may be suffering. Tell him, from his loving mother, that everything is forgiven and forgotten, and that he will find comfort and peace at home.”

On the back of the photograph she had written his full name and address. She had also written down his complexion and the color of his eyes and hair. She had written why he had left home, and what had caused him to do it.
That mother’s parting words were, “When you preach, Mr. Moody, look for my poor boy.”
That young man may be in this hall tonight.
If he is, I want to tell him: your mother still loves you.
I will read out his name. If any of you ever hear of that young man, just tell him that his mother is waiting for him with a loving heart and a tender embrace.
His name is Arthur P. Oxley, of Manchester, England.

Some of you have children all around you. You can feel the pain in the hearts of these families whose greatest joys and delights are gone. Lift up your hearts to God for this father who has gone astray, and for this wandering boy.
If they are still somewhere on the earth, pray that God will turn their hearts and bring them back.
Perhaps no subject in the Bible grips me as strongly as this subject of the wandering sinner.
It touches my own life deeply.
It hits close to home, in our own family.
The first thing I remember is my father’s death.
It was a beautiful day in June when he suddenly fell down dead.
I was young, but the shock made such an impression on me that I will never forget it.
I remember nothing about the funeral, but his death left a lasting mark on me.
The next thing I remember is that my mother became very sick.
And the next thing in our family that stuck in my young mind was this: my oldest brother became a wanderer. He left home. My mother had looked to him to comfort her in her loneliness and deep sorrow.

I don’t need to tell you how that mother grieved for her boy. She waited day after day and month after month for him to come back. I don’t need to tell you how night after night she watched and wept and prayed.
Many times we were sent to the post office to see if a letter had come from him.
But we had to bring back the sad words, “No letter yet, mother.”
Many times I woke up and heard my mother praying, “Oh, God, bring back my boy!”
Many times she lifted up her heart to God in prayer for her boy.

When the winter wind blew around the house and the storm raged outside the door, her dear face looked terribly worried. In a pitiful voice she would say, “Oh, my dear boy! Perhaps he is out on the ocean on this terrible night.
Oh, God, keep him safe!”
In the evenings we would sit around the fire and ask her to tell us about our father. She would talk about him for hours.
But if anyone happened to mention my oldest brother, everyone went quiet. She never spoke of him without tears.
Many times she tried to hide her tears, but it was no use. And when Thanksgiving Day came, a chair was always set for him.
Our friends and neighbors gave up on him, but our mother believed she would see him again.
One day in the middle of summer, someone saw a stranger coming toward the house.
He came up onto the east porch and looked in at my mother through the window.
The man had a long beard. When my mother first saw him, she didn’t jump or get up.
But when she saw the big tears rolling down his cheeks, she cried out, “It’s my boy, my dear, dear boy!” and rushed to the window.
But the boy stood there and said, “Mother, I will never step over the doorstep until you say you forgive me.”
Do you think he had to wait there long?
No, no. Soon her arms were around him, and she wept on his shoulder, just like the father of the prodigal son.
I heard about it while I was in a faraway city, and what a thrill of joy went through me!
But what joy on earth can equal the joy in heaven when a prodigal comes home!
Tonight your father wants you.
Dear son, come to Him.
Confess your sin, and He will have mercy on you and forgive you.
My prayer is that the blessing of heaven will rest on every soul here.
Let us pray.
We read in chapter 15 of Second
Samuel that David was fleeing from Jerusalem as an exile.
Absalom had already weakened David's power and taken his place on the throne.

But as David went through the gate, six hundred men marched on ahead of him. The king said to Ittai, their leader, "Why are you coming with us too? Go back to your place and stay with the king. You are a foreigner, and an exile as well."

Ittai answered the king, "As surely as the Lord lives, and as surely as my lord the king lives, wherever my lord the king is, your servant will be there too. It does not matter whether it means death or life."
There was another man too, named Hushai. He went out to meet the king, but then he went back to the city.
How glad David must have been to find Ittai outside the gate!
Ittai is worth thousands of men like Hushai.
David did not know who his friends were until trouble came.
That act showed true fellowship and true love.
In a time of trouble Ittai would not abandon his king. Instead, he followed him into exile.
That is how it should be in the church.
That is exactly what Christ is looking for. The only thing that can please Him is true love that will leave everything to follow Him.
Some people do not know what the word fellowship means. It means partnership.
Our partnership is with Christ the Son. When we enter into it, everything we have belongs to the firm. We cannot do anything on our own without asking Christ.
We must be like Ittai. We must be willing to leave the city and everything we own, if we have to, so that we can follow Him.
“To know the love of Christ, a love so great that no one can fully understand it.”
(Ephesians 3:19)

The apostle John wrote, “God is love.” If I could only help people understand what those words really mean, I would take that one verse and travel all over the world telling everyone this wonderful truth.
If you can convince someone that you love him, you have won his heart.
If we could really get people to believe that God loves them, we would see them come crowding into the kingdom of heaven!
The problem is that people think God hates them. So they keep running away from Him.
Some years ago we built a church in Chicago. We really wanted to teach the people about God’s love.
We thought, “If we can’t preach it into their hearts, we’ll try to burn it in.” So right above the pulpit we put up the words “God is Love,” spelled out in gas lights.
One night a man walking down the street looked through the door and saw those words.
He was a poor, lost wanderer.
As he walked on, he thought to himself, “God is love!
No! He doesn’t love me. I’m just a poor, miserable sinner.”
He tried to get those words out of his mind. But they seemed to hang right in front of him in letters of fire.
He walked on a little farther. Then he turned around, went back, and went into the meeting.
He didn’t hear the sermon. But the words of that short verse had sunk deep into his heart, and that was enough.
It doesn’t matter much what people say, as long as God’s Word gets into the sinner’s heart.
He stayed after the first meeting was over. I found him there, crying like a child.

I opened the Bible and showed him how God had loved him the whole time, even though he had wandered so far away. I told him God was waiting to welcome him and forgive him. Then the light of the Good News broke into his mind, and he went away full of joy.
Nothing in this world is as precious to people as love.
Show me someone who has nobody to care about him or love him, and I will show you one of the unhappiest people on earth.
Why do people take their own lives?
Very often it is because a thought creeps into their minds that no one loves them. And they would rather die than live.
I don’t know any truth in the whole Bible that should touch us with such power and tenderness as the love of God. And there is no truth in the Bible that Satan would rather wipe out.
For more than six thousand years he has been trying to convince people that God does not love them.
He got the first man and woman to believe this lie. And far too often he gets their children to believe it too.
The idea that God doesn’t love us often comes from wrong teaching.
Mothers make a mistake when they teach their children this: God doesn’t love them when they do wrong, but only when they do right.
The Bible doesn’t teach that.
You don’t teach your children that you hate them when they do wrong.
Their bad behavior doesn’t turn your love into hate. If it did, your love would change a great many times!
When your child is cranky or has disobeyed you, you don’t throw him out as if he didn’t belong to you!
No! He is still your child, and you love him.
In the same way, if people have wandered away from God, that doesn’t mean He hates them.
It is the sin that He hates.
I believe many people think God doesn’t love them because they measure God with their own small ruler. They look at Him only from their own point of view.
We love people as long as we think they deserve our love. When they don’t, we drop them.
God is not like that.
Human love and God’s love are very, very different.
Ephesians 3:18 tells us how wide, how long, how deep, and how high God’s love is.
Many of us think we know something about God’s love. But hundreds of years from now we will admit that we never found out very much about it.
Columbus discovered America. But what did he know about its great lakes, its rivers, its forests, and the Mississippi Valley?
He died without knowing much about what he had discovered.
It’s the same with us. Many of us have discovered something of God’s love. But it has heights and depths and lengths that we still don’t know.
That love is like a huge ocean. We have to dive into it before we really know anything about it.

There is a story about a Roman Catholic Archbishop of Paris. He was thrown into prison and sentenced to be shot. A little while before he was led out to die, he saw a window in his cell shaped like a cross.
At the top of the cross he wrote “height.” At the bottom he wrote “depth.” And at the end of each arm he wrote “length.”
He had experienced the truth in this hymn:

blocks.x:
“When I look at the wonderful cross,
Where the Prince of Glory died.”

s: When we want to know God’s love, we should go to the cross at Calvary.
Can we look at that scene and say that God did not love us?
That cross tells us about God’s love.
No one has ever taught a greater love than the love the cross teaches.
What made God give up Christ? What made Christ die? What else could it be but love?
“No one has greater love than someone who gives up his life for his friends.”

Christ gave up His life for His enemies. Christ gave up His life for the people who killed Him. Christ gave up His life for those who hated Him. The spirit of the cross, the spirit of Calvary, is love.
When they were mocking Him and making fun of Him, what did He say?
“Father, forgive them. They don’t know what they are doing.”
That is love. He did not call down fire from heaven to burn them up. There was nothing but love in His heart.
If you study the Bible, you will find that God’s love never changes.
Many people who once loved you may have cooled off and turned away from you. Maybe their love has even turned into hatred.
God is not like that.

Jesus Christ was about to be taken away from His disciples and led to Calvary. Just then, the Bible tells us, “He had loved His own people in the world, and He loved them all the way to the end” (John 13:1).
He knew that one of His disciples would betray Him. Yet He loved Judas.
He knew that another disciple would deny Him and swear that he had never known Him. And yet He loved Peter.
It was Christ’s love for Peter that broke Peter’s heart. That love brought him back, sorry for what he had done, to the feet of his Lord.
For three years Jesus had been with His disciples, trying to teach them about His love. He taught them not only by His life and words, but also by the things He did.

On the night He was betrayed, He took a bowl of water and wrapped a towel around His waist. He took the place of a servant and washed their feet. He wanted to convince them that His love would never change.
There is no part of the Bible I read as often as John 14. No part is sweeter to me.
I never get tired of reading it.
Listen to what our Lord says as He pours out His heart to His disciples: “On that day you will know that I am in My Father, and you are in Me, and I am in you.
Whoever has My commands and obeys them is the one who loves Me. And whoever loves Me will be loved by My Father” (John 14:20–21).
Just think of it: the great God who made heaven and earth loves you and me! . . .
“If someone loves Me, he will obey My words. My Father will love him, and We will come to him and live with him” (verse 23).
I wish to God that our small minds could grasp this great truth! The Father and the Son love us so much that They want to come and live with us.
Not just to stay for one night, but to come and live in our hearts.
There is an even more wonderful verse in John 17:23.
“I am in them and You are in Me, so that they may be perfectly one. Then the world will know that You sent Me, and that You have loved them just as You have loved Me.”
I think that is one of the most amazing things Jesus Christ ever said.
There is no reason why the Father should not love Him.
He obeyed all the way to death. He never broke the Father’s law. He never stepped off the path of perfect obedience, not even by a hair.
With us it is very different. And yet, in spite of all our rebellion and foolishness, He says that if we trust in Christ, the Father loves us just as He loves the Son.
What amazing love! What wonderful love!
It seems too good to be true that God could love us as much as He loves His own Son.
Yet that is what Jesus Christ teaches.
It is hard to get a sinner to believe that God’s love never changes.
When a man has wandered away from God, he thinks God hates him.
We have to see the difference between the sin and the sinner.
God loves the sinner, but He hates the sin.
He hates sin because it ruins people’s lives.
In fact, God hates sin precisely because He loves the sinner.
God’s love never changes, and it never fails.
In Isaiah 49:15–16 we read: “Can a woman forget the baby at her breast? Could she have no pity for the son she gave birth to? Yes, mothers may forget, but I will not forget you.
Look, I have carved you into the palms of My hands. Your walls are always before My eyes.”
The strongest human love we know is a mother’s love.
Many things can separate a man from his wife.
A father may turn his back on his child. Brothers and sisters may become bitter enemies. Husbands may walk out on their wives, and wives on their husbands.
But a mother’s love lasts through everything.
Whether people speak well or badly of her child, even when the whole world condemns him, a mother keeps on loving. She keeps hoping that her child will turn from his evil ways and be sorry for them.
She remembers his baby smiles, his happy laugh as a little child, and how promising he was as a young man. No one can ever make her think he isn’t worth loving.
Not even death can put out a mother’s love. It is stronger than death.
You have seen a mother watching over her sick child.
How gladly she would take the sickness into her own body if that would make her child well!
Week after week she keeps watch. She won’t let anyone else take care of that sick child.
Some time ago a friend of mine was visiting a beautiful home, where he met a number of friends.
After everyone had left, he realized he had left something behind, so he went back to get it.
There he found the lady of the house, a rich woman, sitting behind a poor man who looked like a tramp.
He was her own son.
Like the prodigal son, he had wandered far away. Yet the mother said, “This is my boy. I still love him.”
Think of a mother with nine or ten children. If one of them goes astray, she seems to love that one more than all the others.
A leading pastor in the state of New York once told me about a father who was a very wicked man.

The mother did everything she could to keep the boy from being spoiled by his father’s evil. But the father’s influence was stronger. He led his son into all kinds of sin, until the young man became one of the worst criminals.
He murdered someone and was put on trial.
All through the trial his mother sat in the courtroom. She was a widow now, because the father had died.
When the witnesses spoke against the boy, it seemed to hurt the mother far more than it hurt her son.
He was found guilty and sentenced to death. Everyone else felt the verdict was fair and seemed satisfied with how things turned out.
But the mother’s love never wavered.
She begged them not to carry out the sentence, but they said no.
After he was executed, she begged to have his body. That was refused too.
As was the custom, he was buried in the prison yard.
A little while later the mother herself died. But before she died, she said she wanted to be buried next to her boy.
She was not ashamed for people to know she was the mother of a murderer.
There is a story about a young woman in Scotland who left her home and ended up living as an outcast in Glasgow.
Her mother searched for her everywhere, but she could not find her.
At last the mother had her own picture hung on the walls of the Midnight Mission rooms, a place where women who lived on the streets used to come.
Many women glanced at the picture as they passed by.
But one stopped and stayed by the picture.
It was the same dear face that had looked down at her when she was a little girl.
Her mother had not forgotten her sinful child or turned her away. Otherwise her picture would never have been hung on those walls.
The lips seemed to open and whisper, “Come home. I forgive you, and I still love you.”
The poor girl sank to the floor, overwhelmed by her feelings.
She was the prodigal daughter.
Seeing her mother’s face had broken her heart.
She became truly sorry for her sins. With a heart full of sorrow and shame, she went back to the home she had left. Mother and daughter were together again.
But let me tell you, no mother’s love can compare with God’s love. It can’t even measure how high or how deep God’s love is.
No mother in this world ever loved her child the way God loves you and me.
Think how much love God must have had when He gave His Son to die for the world.
I used to think much more highly of Christ than I did of the Father.
For some reason I had the idea that God was a harsh judge. I thought Christ had come between me and God to calm God’s anger.

But then I became a father, and for years I had only one son. As I looked at my boy, I thought about the Father giving His Son to die. It seemed to me that it took more love for the Father to give His Son than for the Son to die.
Oh, how much God must have loved the world when He gave His Son to die for it!
“God loved the world so much that He gave His only Son, so that whoever believes in Him will not be lost but will have life that lasts forever” (John 3:16).
I have never been able to preach a sermon on that verse.
I have often thought I would. But it is so high that I can never climb to the top of it. I have just quoted it and moved on.
Who can measure how deep those words are: “God loved the world so much”?
We can never climb to the top of His love or reach the bottom of it.
Paul prayed that he could know how high, how deep, how long, and how wide God’s love is. But he could not figure it all out.
It is “too great to understand” (Ephesians 3:19).
Nothing shows us God’s love like the cross of Christ.
Come with me to Calvary and look at the Son of God as He hangs there.
Can you hear that piercing cry from His dying lips, “Father, forgive them. They don’t know what they are doing!” and still say that He doesn’t love you?
“No one has greater love than someone who gives up his life for his friends” (John 15:13).
But Jesus Christ gave up His life for His enemies.
Here is another thought: He loved us long before we ever thought about Him.
The Bible never says that He won’t love us until we love Him first.
In 1 John 4:10
it says: “This is love: not that we loved God, but that He loved us and sent His Son to be the sacrifice for our sins.”
He loved us before we ever thought of loving Him.
You loved your children before they knew anything about your love.
In the same way, long before we ever thought about God, He was thinking about us.
What brought the prodigal son home?
It was the thought that his father loved him.
Suppose he had heard that his father had disowned him and didn’t care about him anymore. Would he have gone back?
Never! But then it dawned on him that his father still loved him. So he got up and went back home.
Dear reader, the Father’s love should bring us back to Him.
It was Adam’s disaster and sin that showed God’s love.
When Adam fell into sin, God came down and treated him with mercy.
If anyone is lost, it won’t be because God doesn’t love him. It will be because he has pushed away God’s love.
What will make heaven so attractive?
Is it the gates of pearl or the streets of gold?
No. Heaven will be attractive because there we will see the One who loved us so much that He gave His only Son to die for us.
What makes a home attractive?
Is it beautiful furniture and grand rooms?
No. Some homes that have all these things are like graves painted white.
In Brooklyn a mother was dying. They had to take her child away from her, because the little girl couldn’t understand how sick her mother was, and she kept disturbing her.
Every night the child cried herself to sleep at a neighbor’s house, because she wanted to go back to her mother. But the mother got worse, and they couldn’t take the child home.
At last the mother died. After she died, they thought it was best not to let the child see her mother lying dead in her coffin.

After the funeral the child ran into one room crying, “Mommy! Mommy!” and then into another room crying, “Mommy! Mommy!” She went through the whole house like that. When the little girl couldn’t find the one she loved, she cried to be taken back to the neighbors.
In the same way, what makes heaven attractive is knowing that we will see Christ, who loved us and gave Himself for us.
If you ask me why God loves us, I can’t tell you.
I suppose it is because He is a true Father.
It is His nature to love, just as it is the sun’s nature to shine.
He wants you to share in that love.
Don’t let unbelief keep you away from Him.
Don’t think that God doesn’t love you or care about you just because you are a sinner.
He does! He wants to save you and bless you.
“When we had no strength of our own, Christ died for ungodly people at the time God chose” (Romans 5:6).
Isn’t that enough to convince you that He loves you?
He would not have died for you if He didn’t love you.
Is your heart so hard that you can set yourself against His love and push it away with scorn?
You can do it, but you will be putting yourself in great danger.
I can imagine some of you thinking, “Yes, we believe God loves us if we love Him. We believe God loves people who are pure and holy.”
Let me tell you, my friend, God doesn’t only love the pure and holy. He also loves the ungodly.
“God shows how much He loves us by this: Christ died for us while we were still sinners” (Romans 5:8).
God sent Him to die for the sins of the whole world.
If you are part of the world, then you have a share in this love that was shown on the cross of Christ.
There is a verse in Revelation 1:5
that means a great deal to me: “To Him who loved us and washed us.”
You might think God would wash us first and then love us.
But no, He loved us first.
About eight years ago the whole country was deeply upset about Charlie Ross, a four-year-old boy who was kidnapped.
Two men in a small horse-drawn carriage asked him and his older brother if they wanted some candy.
Then they drove off with the younger boy and left the older one behind.
For many years people have searched for him in every state and territory.
Men have gone to Great Britain, France, and Germany and hunted for the child, but they never found him.
His mother still lives in hope that she will see her long-lost Charlie again.
I don’t remember the whole country ever being so stirred up about anything, except perhaps the murder of President Garfield.
Now suppose Charlie Ross’s mother was at a meeting. While the preacher was speaking, she happened to look down into the crowd and saw her long-lost son.
Suppose he was poor, dirty, and in rags, with no shoes and no coat. What would she do?
Would she wait until he was washed and dressed properly before she would admit he was hers?
No! She would get down from the platform right away, rush over to him, and take him in her arms.
After that she would wash him and give him clothes.
That is how God is.
He loved us, and He washed us.
I can imagine someone saying, “If God loves me, why doesn’t He make me good?”
God wants sons and daughters in heaven. He doesn’t want machines or slaves.
He could break our stubborn hearts. But He wants to draw us to Himself with the ropes of love.
He wanted you to sit down with Him at the wedding feast of the Lamb. He wanted to wash you and make you whiter than snow.
He wants you to walk with Him on the crystal streets of that happy world beyond.
He wants to adopt you into His family and make you a son or daughter of heaven.
Will you trample His love under your feet? Or will you give yourself to Him right now, this very hour?
During our terrible Civil War, a mother got the news that her son had been wounded in the Battle of the Wilderness.
She took the first train and set out to find her boy. But the War Department had given an order that no more women were allowed past the army lines.
A mother’s love doesn’t care about orders, though. By crying and begging, she managed to get through the lines to the Wilderness.
At last she found the hospital where her boy was.
She went to the doctor and said, “Will you let me go into the ward and take care of my boy?”
The doctor said, “I have just gotten your son to sleep. He is in very serious condition. I’m afraid that if you wake him up, the excitement will be so great that it will kill him.
You had better wait a while and stay outside. Let me tell him you have come, so I can break the news to him slowly.”
The mother looked into the doctor’s face and said, “Doctor, what if my boy never wakes up, and I never see him alive?
Let me go and sit beside him. I won’t say a word to him.”
“If you won’t speak to him, you may go,” said the doctor.
She tiptoed to his bed and looked into her boy’s face.
How she had longed to see him!
How her eyes seemed to feast on him as she gazed at his face!
When she got close enough, she couldn’t keep her hands off him. She laid her tender, loving hand on his forehead.
The moment her hand touched her boy’s forehead, he cried out without even opening his eyes, “Mother, you’ve come!”
He knew the touch of that loving hand.
There was love and sympathy in it.
Oh, sinner, if you feel the loving touch of Jesus, you will recognize it. It is so full of tenderness.
The world may treat you unkindly, but Christ never will.
You will never have a better Friend in this world.
What you need to do is come to Him today.
Let His loving arm hold you up from underneath. Let His loving hand be around you. He will hold you with mighty power.
He will keep you safe and fill your heart with His tenderness and love.
I can imagine some of you asking, “How should I go to Him?”
Why, just the way you would go to your mother.
Have you badly hurt your mother and done her a great wrong?
If so, you go to her and say, “Mother, I want you to forgive me.”
Treat Christ the same way.
Go to Him today. Tell Him that you haven’t loved Him and haven’t treated Him right. Confess your sins, and see how quickly He will bless you.
This reminds me of another story. It is about a boy who had been tried by a military court and sentenced to be shot.
His father and mother were heartbroken when they heard the news.
A little girl lived in that home.
She had read about the life of Abraham Lincoln. She said, “If Abraham Lincoln knew how much my father and mother love their boy, he wouldn’t let my brother be shot.”
She wanted her father to go to Washington and beg for his son’s life.
But her father said, “No, it’s no use. The law must take its course.

They have already refused to pardon one or two others who were sentenced by that military court. And an order has gone out that the President won’t step in again. If a man has been sentenced by a military court, he has to suffer the consequences.”
That father and mother didn’t have the faith to believe their boy might be pardoned.
But the little girl was full of hope. She got on the train far up in Vermont and set off for Washington.
When she reached the White House, the soldiers wouldn’t let her in. But she told them her sad story, and they let her through.
Then she came to the room where the President’s private secretary worked. He refused to let her into the President’s private office.
But the little girl told her story, and it touched the secretary’s heart. So he let her go in.

When she walked into Abraham Lincoln’s room, there were U.S. senators, generals, governors, and important politicians there on serious business about the war. But the President happened to see that child standing at his door.
He asked what she wanted. She went right up to him and told her story in her own words.
He was a father, and big tears rolled down Abraham Lincoln’s cheeks.
He wrote a message and sent it to the army, ordering them to send that boy to Washington at once.
When the boy arrived, the President pardoned him, gave him thirty days of leave, and sent him home with the little girl to cheer up his father and mother.
Do you want to know how to go to Christ?
Go just the way that little girl went to Abraham Lincoln.
Maybe you have a dark story to tell.
Tell all of it. Don’t hold anything back.
Abraham Lincoln had compassion on that little girl. He listened to her request and said yes to it. So do you think the Lord Jesus won’t hear your prayer?
Do you think Abraham Lincoln, or anyone who ever lived on earth, had as much compassion as Christ?
No! He will be moved when no one else is. He will show mercy when no one else will. He will have pity when no one else will.
If you go straight to Him and confess your sin and your need, He will save you.
A few years ago a man left England and moved to America.
He was English, but he became an American citizen.

A few years later he grew restless and unhappy, so he went to Cuba. He had been in Cuba only a short time when a civil war broke out there. This was in 1867. The Spanish government arrested the man as a spy.
He was tried by a military court, found guilty, and sentenced to be shot.
The whole trial was held in Spanish, so the poor man had no idea what was going on.

When they told him the verdict—that he was guilty and sentenced to be shot—he sent word to the American consul and the English consul. He told them everything, proved he was innocent, and asked them to protect him.

They looked into the case and found that the man the Spanish officers had sentenced to be shot was completely innocent. They went to the Spanish general and said, “Listen, this man you have sentenced to death is innocent. He is not guilty.”
But the Spanish general said, “He has been tried by our law. He has been found guilty. He must die.”
There was no telegraph cable, so these men could not get in touch with their governments.
The morning came when the man was to be executed.
He was brought out sitting on his own coffin in a cart and taken to the place of execution.
A grave was dug.
They took the coffin off the cart and sat the young man on it. They took the black hood and were just pulling it down over his face.
The Spanish soldiers were waiting for the order to fire.
But just then the American and English consuls rode up.

The English consul jumped out of the carriage, took the Union Jack—the British flag—and wrapped it around the man. The American consul wrapped the Star-Spangled Banner around him. Then they turned to the Spanish officers and said, “Fire on those flags if you dare!”
They did not dare to fire on those flags.
Two great nations stood behind those flags.
That was the secret.
“He brought me into the banquet hall, and His banner over me was love. . . .
His left hand supports my head, and His right hand holds me close” (Song of Solomon 2:4, 6).
Thank God, we can come under that banner today if we want to.
Any poor sinner can come under that banner today.
His banner of love is over us.
What blessed Good News! What blessed, precious news!
Believe it today. Take it into your heart. And begin a new life.
Let the Holy Spirit pour God’s love into your heart today. It will drive away the darkness. It will drive away the gloom. It will drive away sin. And you will have peace and joy.
The next subject is perhaps the hardest of all to deal with. It is forgiveness.
I believe this keeps more people from having power with God than anything else. They are not willing to develop a forgiving spirit.
If we let a root of bitterness grow up in our hearts against someone, our prayer will not be answered.
It may not be easy to live in sweet fellowship with everyone we come in contact with. But that is exactly what God gives us His grace for.
The disciples’ prayer is a test of whether we are God’s sons. If we can pray all of it from the heart, we have good reason to believe that we have been born of God.
No one can call God Father except by the Spirit.
This prayer has been a great blessing to the world. Yet I believe it has also been a great trap. Many people stumble over it and are lost.
They don’t think about what it means. They don’t take its truths deep into their hearts.
I have no sympathy for the idea that all people are sons of God.
The Bible teaches very clearly that we are adopted into God’s family.
If everyone were already a son, God would not need to adopt anyone.
We all belong to God because He created us. But some people teach that anyone can say, “Our Father in heaven,” whether he is born of God or not. I think that goes against Scripture.
“All who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God.”
Being a son in God’s family is the privilege of the believer.
The apostle says, “By this the children of God and the children of the devil are made plain.”
If we are doing God’s will, that is a very good sign that we are born of God.
If we have no desire to do His will, how can we call God “Our Father”?
Here is another thing. We cannot really pray for God’s kingdom to come until we are in it.
Suppose we pray for God’s kingdom to come while we are rebelling against Him. Then we are only asking for our own condemnation.
No one whose heart has not been made new really wants God’s will to be done on earth.
Over the door of every unsaved person’s house, and over his place of business, you could write: “God’s will is not done here.”
If the nations really prayed this prayer, they could send all their armies home.
We are told there are about twelve million men in the standing armies of Europe alone.
But people don’t want God’s will done on earth as it is in heaven. That is the problem.
Now let’s come to the part I want to spend time on: “Forgive us the wrongs we have done, as we forgive those who have wronged us.”
This is the only part of the prayer that Christ explained.
“If you forgive people the wrongs they do, your heavenly Father will forgive you too. But if you don’t forgive people their wrongs, your Father will not forgive your wrongs.”
Notice this: when you go through the door into God’s kingdom, you go in through the door of forgiveness.
I have never known anyone to receive a blessing in his own soul if he was not willing to forgive others.
If we are unwilling to forgive others, God cannot forgive us.
I don’t see how words could be any plainer than these words of our Lord.
I truly believe that a great many prayers are not answered because we are not willing to forgive someone.
Think back over the past. Go through all the people you know. Is there anyone you hold hard feelings against?
Is a root of bitterness growing in you against someone who may have hurt you?
Maybe you have been nursing this unforgiving spirit for months or even years. How can you ask God to forgive you?
Suppose I am not willing to forgive people who may have wronged me just once. How mean and shameful it would be for me to ask God to forgive the ten thousand sins I am guilty of!
But Christ goes even further.

He says: “If you bring your gift to the altar and remember there that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there in front of the altar and go. First make peace with your brother. Then come and offer your gift.”
Maybe you are saying, “I don’t think I have anything against anyone.”
Does anyone have something against you?
Is there someone who thinks you have wronged them?
Maybe you haven’t. But they may think you have.
I’ll tell you what I would do before I go to sleep tonight. I would go and see them and get the matter settled.
You will find that you are greatly blessed in the very act of doing it.
Suppose you are in the right and they are in the wrong. You may win over your brother or sister.
May God pull this unforgiving spirit out of all our hearts by the roots.
Some time ago a man came to me. He wanted me to talk to his wife about her soul.
She seemed as eager as anyone I had ever met. I thought it would not take long to lead her into the light. But the longer I talked with her, the darker things seemed to get for her.
I went to see her again the next day. I found her in even greater darkness of soul.
I thought something must be standing in the way that I had not yet found. So I asked her to say the disciples’ prayer with me.
I thought that if she could say this prayer from the heart, the Lord would meet her with peace.
I began to say it one sentence at a time, and she repeated each one after me. Then I came to this request: “Forgive us the wrongs we have done, as we forgive those who have wronged us.”
There she stopped. I said it a second time and waited for her to repeat it. She said she could not do it.
“What is the problem?”
She answered, “There is one woman I will never forgive.”
“Oh,” I said, “now I see what’s wrong. There is no use in my going on to pray. Your prayers will not go any higher than my head.
God says He will not forgive you unless you forgive others.
If you do not forgive this woman, God will never forgive you.
That is what heaven has decided.”
She said, “Are you saying that I cannot be forgiven until I have forgiven her?”
“No, I am not saying it. The Lord says it, and He is a far better authority.”
She said, “Then I will never be forgiven.”
I left the house without having made any impression on her.
A few years later I heard that this woman was in a mental asylum.
I believe this unforgiving spirit drove her insane.
If someone has something against you, go right away and make peace with them.
If you have something against anyone, write them a letter. Tell them that you forgive them. That way you will get this thing off your conscience.
I remember being in the inquiry room some years ago. I was in one corner of the room, talking with a young woman.
Something seemed to be in the way, but I could not find out what it was.
At last I asked, “Isn’t there someone you are not forgiving?”
She looked up at me and said, “Why did you ask that?
Has someone told you about me?”
“No,” I said. “But I thought that might be the case, because you have not received forgiveness yourself.”
“Well,” she said, pointing to another corner of the room, where a young woman was sitting, “I have had trouble with that young woman. We haven’t spoken to each other for a long time.”
“Oh,” I said, “now it is all clear to me. You cannot be forgiven until you are willing to forgive her.”
It was a hard struggle.
But you know, the greater the cross, the greater the blessing.
To make mistakes is human. But to forgive and be forgiven is like Christ.
At last this young woman said, “I will go and forgive her.”
Strangely enough, the same struggle was going on in the mind of the woman in the other part of the room.
They both came to their senses at about the same time.
They met each other in the middle of the room.
One of them tried to say that she forgave the other, but they could not finish. So they rushed into each other’s arms.
Then the four of us—the two seekers and the two workers—knelt down together, and we had a wonderful meeting.
These two went away full of joy.
Dear friend, is this why your prayers are not being answered?
Is there a friend, a family member, or someone in the church that you have not forgiven?
Sometimes we hear of members of the same church who have not spoken to each other for years.
How can we expect God to forgive when that is the case?
I remember one town that Mr. Sankey and I visited.
For a week it felt as if we were just beating the air. There was no power in the meetings.
Finally, one day I said that perhaps someone was holding on to this unforgiving spirit.
The chairman of our committee was sitting next to me. He got up and left the meeting in full view of the audience.
The arrow had hit its target. It had gone straight to the heart of the committee chairman.
He had been in conflict with someone for about six months.
He went at once to find this man and asked him to forgive him.
He came to me with tears in his eyes and said, “I thank God you ever came here.”
That night the inquiry room was crowded.
The chairman became one of the best workers I have ever known. He has been active in Christian service ever since.
Several years ago the Church of England sent a devoted missionary to New Zealand.
He worked hard there for a few years, and his work was successful. Then one Sunday he was leading a communion service in an area where the converts had been savages not long before.
As the missionary was leading the service, he noticed one of the men. Just as the man was about to kneel at the rail, he suddenly jumped up and hurried to the opposite end of the church.
After a while he came back and calmly took his place.
After the service the minister took him aside and asked him why he had acted so strangely.

He answered: “As I was about to kneel, I recognized the man next to me. He was the chief of a neighboring tribe. He had murdered my father and drunk his blood. And I had sworn by all the gods that I would kill that man at the first chance I got.
At first the urge to take revenge almost overpowered me. So I rushed away, as you saw, to escape its power.
I stood at the other end of the room and thought about why we were meeting. Then I thought of Him who prayed for His own murderers: ‘Father, forgive them, for they don’t know what they are doing.’
And I felt that I could forgive the man who murdered my father. So I came back and knelt down beside him.”
As someone has said: “There is an ugly kind of forgiveness in the world. It is a kind of hedgehog forgiveness, shot out like quills.

People take someone who has offended them and set him in front of the blowtorch of their anger. They scorch him and burn his fault into him. And when they have kneaded him enough with their fists, then they forgive him.”
The father of Frederick the Great was on his deathbed. His spiritual adviser, M. Roloff, warned him that he must forgive his enemies.

This troubled him a great deal. After a moment he said to the Queen: “Feekin, after I am dead you may write to your brother (the King of England). Tell him that I forgave him and died at peace with him.”
M. Roloff gently suggested, “It would be better for Your Majesty to write now.”
“No,” was the stern answer.
“Write after I am dead.
That will be safer.”
Another story tells of a man who thought he was about to die. He told someone who had hurt him that he forgave him. But then he added, “Now remember, if I get well, the old grudge still stands.”
My friends, that is not forgiveness at all.
I believe true forgiveness includes forgetting the offense. It means putting it completely out of our hearts and memories.
As Matthew Henry says: “We do not forgive our brother who has offended us in the right way, or in a way God accepts, unless we forgive him from the heart. For that is what God looks at.

No hatred must be kept there, and no ill will toward anyone. No plans for revenge must be hatched there, and no desire for it. Yet such things are there in many who look peaceful and reconciled on the outside.
From the heart we must desire and seek the good of those who have offended us.”
If God forgave the way we often do, His forgiveness would not be worth much.
Suppose God said, “I will forgive you, but I will never forget it. All through eternity I will keep reminding you of it.” We would not feel that was forgiveness at all.
Notice what God says: “I will remember their sin no more.”
In a passage in Ezekiel it says that not one of our sins will be mentioned. Isn’t that just like God?
I love to preach this forgiveness. It is the sweet truth that sin is blotted out for time and eternity, and it will never once be mentioned against us.
In another passage of Scripture we read: “I will remember their sins and iniquities no more.”
Then turn to the eleventh chapter of Hebrews and read God’s honor roll. You will find that not one of the sins of those men of faith is mentioned.
Abraham is called the man of faith. But it does not tell how he denied his wife down in Egypt. All that had been forgiven.
Moses was kept out of the Promised Land because he lost his patience. But the New Testament does not mention this, even though his name is on the apostle’s honor roll.
Samson is named too, but his sins are not brought up again.
Why, we even read of “righteous Lot.” In the Old Testament story he did not look much like a righteous man. But he has been forgiven, and God has made him “righteous.”
Once God has forgiven us, our sins will never again be remembered against us.
This is God’s eternal decree.

Brooks speaks of the pardon God gives His people: “When God pardons sin, He takes it completely away. Even if someone searched for it, it could not be found. As the prophet Jeremiah says: ‘In those days and at that time, says the Lord, people will search for the iniquity of Israel, but there will be none; and for the sins of Judah, but they will not be found; for I will pardon those I preserve.’

When David saw in Mephibosheth the features of his friend Jonathan, he took no notice of his lameness or any other defect or deformity. In the same way, when God sees in His people the glorious image of His Son, He overlooks all their faults and deformities. This made Luther say, ‘Do with me what You want, since You have pardoned my sin.’
And what is pardoning sin, except no longer mentioning it?”
We read in the Gospel of Matthew: “Also, if your brother sins against you, go and show him his fault, just between the two of you. If he listens to you, you have gained your brother.”
A little further on we read that Peter comes to Christ and asks, “How often should I forgive my brother when he sins against me?
Up to seven times?” Jesus answered, “I don’t say up to seven times, but up to seventy times seven.”
Peter did not seem to think he was in danger of falling into sin. His question was, “How often should I forgive my brother?”
But very soon we hear that Peter has fallen.
I can imagine that when he did fall, a sweet thought came to him. He remembered what the Master had said about forgiving up to seventy times seven.
The voice of sin may be loud, but the voice of forgiveness is louder.
Let us enter into David’s experience when he said: “Blessed is the one whose wrongdoing is forgiven, whose sin is covered.
Blessed is the man whose sin the Lord does not count against him, and whose spirit has no deceit.
When I kept silent, my bones grew old from my crying out all day long.
Day and night Your hand was heavy on me. The moisture in me was turned into the dryness of summer.
I admitted my sin to You and did not hide my wrongdoing.
I said, ‘I will confess my wrongdoings to the Lord.’ And You forgave the wickedness of my sin.”
David could look down and up, back and ahead—to the past, the present, and the future—and know that all was well.
Let us decide that we will not rest until this question of sin is settled forever. Then we can look up and claim God as our forgiving Father.

Let us be willing to forgive others, so that we can claim forgiveness from God. Let us remember the words of the Lord Jesus, when He said: “If you forgive people the wrongs they do, your heavenly Father will forgive you too. But if you don’t forgive people their wrongs, your Father will not forgive your wrongs.”
No doubt you have often read the story of the good Samaritan.
In this parable Christ shows us four men.
He paints the picture so clearly that the world will never forget it.
But too often, when we read the stories in the Bible, they don’t touch our hearts. Before long we forget the lesson the Master wants us to learn and remember.
When Christ was on earth, there was a group of people who gathered around Him. They kept finding fault with everything He said and did.
We read that on this occasion an expert in the law came and asked Him what he could do to inherit eternal life.
Our Lord told him to keep the commandments: to love the Lord with all his heart, and to love his neighbor as himself.
Then the expert in the law wanted to know who his neighbor was.
In this story Christ told him who his neighbor was, and what it meant to love him.
It seems to me that we have taken a long time to figure out who our neighbor is.

I think that in the parable of the good Samaritan, Christ has taught us very clearly who our neighbor is. It is any man or woman who needs our love and our help, whether for this life or for the soul.
If we can do anything to help them, we should do it in the name of our Master.
Here we are shown two men. Each of them passed by someone in great need. That man had been attacked by robbers. They had stripped him, wounded him, and left him there to die.
The first person who came down that road from Jerusalem to Jericho was a priest.
As he walked along the road, he heard a cry for help. He looked to see who the unfortunate man was.
He could see that the poor man was a Jew. Maybe he had even seen him in the temple on the Sabbath.
But he was not in his own parish now.
His work was in the temple, and it was finished for now.
He was a professional. He had done everything that was required of him.
He was in a great hurry to get down to Jericho.
Maybe they were going to open a new synagogue there, and he was supposed to dedicate it.
That was very important business. So of course he couldn’t stop to help this poor, wounded man who had been knocked down.
So he kept going.
Maybe as he walked along, he reasoned with himself something like this: “I wonder why God ever let sin come into the world at all.
It is very strange that people should be in this fallen condition.”
Or maybe his thoughts went another way. He told himself that when he got to Jericho, he would set up a committee to look after these unfortunate brothers.
He would give some money toward the costs.
Or he would try to get a policeman to go after the robbers who had stripped the man.
He didn’t stop to think that all this time the poor wounded man was dying.
Most likely the man was crying out for water. Maybe there was even a stream running by, just a stone’s throw from where he lay.
Still, this priest never stopped to give him a drink.
All his religion was in his head. It had never reached his heart.
The only thing on his mind was duty, duty. When he had finished what he thought was his duty, he imagined his work was done.
God wants us to serve Him from the heart. If we don’t give Him that, we can’t serve Him at all.
We read that next a Levite came along the road where the wounded man was lying helpless.
As he passed by, he too heard the man crying for help.
He stepped aside for a moment to look at the poor man. He could see that he was a son of Abraham, a fellow Jew.
But he also had to hurry on to Jericho.
Maybe he had to help with the ceremony for opening the new synagogue.
Or maybe there was going to be a conference down there on “How to Reach the Masses,” and he was going to help discuss the topic.
I have noticed that many men today will go to a conference and talk for hours about that subject. But they won’t lift a hand themselves to reach the masses.
The Levite’s thoughts probably went another way. He said to himself, “I’ll see if I can get the Legislature to pass a law to stop those robbers from robbing and wounding people.”
Some people today think they can make laws that will bring people back to God. They think they can stop sin by making laws.
Like the priest, this Levite never stopped to give the poor man a drop of water for his thirst. He never tried to bandage his wounds or help him in any way.
He went on down the road, no doubt saying to himself, “I feel sorry for that poor man.”
There is a lot of that kind of pity today. But it comes only from the lips, not from the heart.
The next person to come along that road was a Samaritan.
Now everyone knew that in those days a Jew would not speak to a Samaritan. To a strict Jew, just being near a Samaritan made him unclean.
No Jew ever went into the home of a hated Samaritan. He would not eat at his table or drink from his well.
And he would not let a Samaritan come into his house.
No religious Jew would even buy from a Samaritan or sell to him.
You know a Jew must think very poorly of a man if he won’t do business with him when there’s a chance of making money from him.
Not only that, the Jews believed that Samaritans had no souls. They thought that when Samaritans died, they would simply cease to exist.
Their graves would be so deep that not even the sound of Gabriel’s trumpet would wake them on the morning of the resurrection.
The Samaritan was the only man under heaven who could not convert to the Jewish faith and become part of the Jewish family.
He was not allowed to repent, in this life or in the life to come.
He might claim to follow the Jewish religion, but they would have nothing to do with him.
That was how they looked at these people. Yet Christ used the despised Samaritan to teach these bitter Jews the lesson of loving their neighbor.
The Samaritan came that way.
The story says that the priest came down that way “by chance.” But it doesn’t say that the Samaritan came by chance.
He stands for our Lord and Master.
We are told that he came to where the poor wounded man was. He got down from the animal he was riding and bent down right there beside the hurt man.
He looked at him and saw that he was a Jew.
If he had been like the Jews themselves, he probably would have said, “Serves you right.
I only wish the robbers had killed you on the spot.
I wouldn’t lift a finger to help you, you poor miserable Samaritan.”
But no! He didn’t say a single word of judgment or blame.
Let’s learn a lesson from this.
Do you think these drunkards need anyone to condemn them?
No one in the whole world can condemn them the way they condemn themselves.
What they need is sympathy: tenderness, gentleness, and kindness.
This Samaritan didn’t pull a manuscript out of his pocket and start reading a long sermon to the wounded man.
Some people seem to think that all the world needs is lots of sermons.
Why, the people of this country have almost been preached to death!
What we need is to preach more sermons with our hands and feet. We need to carry the Gospel to people by acts of kindness.
He also didn’t give this poor Jew a long lecture trying to prove that science was better than religion.
He didn’t give him a long talk about geology. What good would that do him?
What the poor man needed was sympathy and help.
So the first thing the good Samaritan did was pour oil into his wounds.
There are so many wounded people among us who need the oil of pity and sympathy!
Many Christians seem to carry a bottle of vinegar with them all the time. And they bring it out at every chance.
The Samaritan could have said to the man, “Why didn’t you stay in Jerusalem?
What were you doing on this road anyway, causing all this trouble?”
People sometimes do the same thing to a young man who has come to the city and gotten into trouble. They say to him, “Why did you ever leave home and come to this wicked city?”
They start to scold him and blame him.
You will never reach people and do them good that way. Nor will you do it by standing on a high platform. You have to come down to them and share in their sorrows and troubles.
See how this Samaritan “came to where he was.” Instead of lecturing him, he poured healing oil into his wounds.
Notice that the story mentions twelve things the Samaritan did.
We can sum up in one word everything the priest and the Levite did: nothing.
(1.) He “came to where he was.”
(2.) He “saw him.” He did not pass by on the other side, as the priest did.
(3.) He “felt compassion for him.”
If we want to succeed in winning souls, we too must be moved with compassion for people who are lost and perishing.
We must share people’s sorrows and troubles if we hope to win their hearts and do them good.
(4.) He “went to him.”
The Levite went toward him. But we are told that he, like the priest, “passed by on the other side.”
(5.) He “bandaged his wounds.”
Maybe he had to tear up his own clothes to do it.
(6.) He poured in oil, and he gave some wine to the man, who was fainting.
(7.) He “put him on his own animal.”
Don’t you think this poor Jew must have looked at the Samaritan with thankfulness and tender feelings? He was sitting on the animal while the man who rescued him walked beside him.
All the prejudice in his heart must have disappeared long before they reached the end of their trip.
(8.) He “took him to an inn.”
(9.) He “took care of him.”
I was deeply moved when I heard about a Christian worker in one of the parts of London where we were. He met a man at the meeting who had been drinking.
He saw that the man was drunk. So he took him home and stayed with him all night. Then the next morning, when the man was sober, he talked with him.

Many people are quite willing to talk with drunkards when they are sober. But very few will go and look for them when they are in their fallen condition. Very few will stay with them until they are able to talk sensibly about their salvation.
(10.) When the good Samaritan left the next day, he asked the innkeeper to take care of the man.
(11.) He gave him some money to pay the bill.
(12.) He said, “If you spend more than this, I will pay you back when I come again.”
I think nothing in all of Christ’s teaching shows the whole Gospel better than this parable.
It is a perfect picture of Christ coming down to this world to seek and save the lost.

(1.) He came to this world of sin and sorrow where we were. For a time He laid aside His glory. He did this so that He could take on our human nature and put Himself on the same level as those He came to save.
(2.) He spent time with the poor and needy so that He could see how they lived.
(3.) He was “moved with compassion” for the crowds. The Gospels tell us this again and again.
We are told more than once that He wept as He thought about all the misery and pain that sin had brought on the human family.
(4.) Whenever Jesus Christ heard of someone in sorrow or need, He went right away.
No one ever cried to Him for help in vain.
(5.) Once He read from the prophets about Himself: “The Spirit of the Lord is on me . . . because the Lord has . . . sent me to bind up those whose hearts are broken.”
He Himself was wounded so that the wounds sin had made in us could be bandaged and healed.
(6.) He not only comforted those who were sad. He also promised the Holy Spirit, who would bring comfort and strength to His redeemed people.
(7.) The good Samaritan put the wounded man on his own animal. In the same way, the Savior gives us the promise of His word that never fails. We can rest on it during our journey as pilgrims.
He Himself has promised to be with us in spirit along the way.
(8.) He brings us to a place of rest. We rest in His love, in His willingness to save, and in His power to keep us.
In the end He will bring us to our home of rest that lasts forever.
(9.) When He was on earth, He took a personal interest in everything that mattered to His disciples, and
(10.) When He had gone up to heaven, He sent another Comforter who would stay with the Church.
(11.) He has given the Church everything she needs to be supported and to grow in grace.
(12.) He will come again and reward His servants for all their faithful service.
Do you want to know how you can reach the masses?
Go to their homes and show them sympathy. Tell them you have come to do them good. Let them see that your heart really feels for them.
When they find out that you truly love them, all the things in their hearts against God and against Christianity will be swept away.
Atheists may tell them that you only want their money, and that you don’t really care whether they are happy.
We have to prove that lie wrong by the way we live. We have to send it back to the pit it came from.
We won’t do it unless we go to them in person and prove that we really love them.
There are hundreds and thousands of families who could easily be reached. We just need thousands of Christians to go to them and share in their sorrows.
That is what they want.
This poor world is groaning and sighing for sympathy—human sympathy.
I am quite sure that this was what touched the hearts of the common people in Christ’s life.
He made Himself one with them.
He was rich, yet for our sakes He became poor.
He was born in the manger so that He could put Himself on the same level as the very lowest people.
I think He is teaching His disciples a lesson in this.
He wants us to convince the world that He is their friend.
They don’t believe it.
If the world ever grasped this truth—that Jesus Christ is the Friend of sinners—they would soon come flocking to Him.
I am sure that ninety-nine out of every hundred people who don’t belong to Christ think that God hates them instead of loving them.
How will they find out they are wrong?
They don’t come to our churches. And even if they did, in many places they would not hear it.

Think of the poor prostitutes walking the streets of our cities. Suppose they really believed that Jesus Christ loved them and wanted to be their friend. Suppose they believed that if He were here in person, He would not condemn them, but would take their side and try to lift them up. Do you think they would keep on sinning?
Do you think the poor drunkard staggering down the street really believes that Christ is his friend and loves him?
The Bible clearly teaches that even though Christ hates sin, He loves the sinner.
This story of the good Samaritan was given to teach us this lesson.
Let’s spread the good news everywhere that Christ loves sinners and came into the world to save them.
There was once a man who lived in one of our large cities.
He died quite suddenly. Not long after, his wife followed him to the grave.
They left two boys. A wealthy man in the city took the more promising boy and adopted him.
The other boy was put in the orphanage.
While his parents were alive, he had never been away from them. And he had never been separated from his brother before.
Every night he cried himself to sleep, missing his brother.
One night they couldn’t find him.
The next morning they found him under the steps of the house of the rich banker who had adopted his little brother.
They asked him why he had left a good, comfortable bed at the orphanage to stay out there all night in the cold. He said he wanted to be near Charlie.
He knew that if he rang the bell and they found him at the door, they would send him back. It comforted him to be near Charlie, even if he had to spend the night outside.
His young heart longed for sympathy. He knew that Charlie loved him more than anyone else in the world did.
If we can just convince these poor lost people that someone loves them, their hearts will be moved.
During the war a little boy named Frankie Bragg was put in one of the hospitals.
He said it was so hard to be there, far away from everyone who loved him.
The nurse who was caring for him bent down, kissed him, and told him she loved him.
“Do you love me?” he asked. “Kiss me again. That was like my sister’s kiss.”
The nurse kissed him again. Then he smiled and said, “It isn’t hard for me to die now, when I know that someone loves me.”
