If we had more of this sympathy for those who are lost and grieving, the world would soon feel our influence.
Shouldn’t we learn a lesson from the good Samaritan?
Let’s listen to the voice of the Master saying, “Go and do the same.”
We can all do something.
If we can’t reach the older people, let’s try to win the young.
It is a blessed privilege to be used by God to bring even one little lamb into the kingdom.
If we help save just one child, our life will not be a failure. We will hear the Master say, “Well done, good and faithful servant.”
Two years ago a lady started a hospital in Edinburgh for sick and crippled children.
I asked her if she had been blessed in the work.
I will never forget how her face lit up.
She came to one of our recent meetings in London, and her face was shining with joy.
She was telling about some very interesting cases of children who had been converted.
What a privilege it is to lead these suffering ones into the kingdom of God!
A little boy was brought to Edinburgh from Fife.
There was no room in the children’s hospital, so he was taken to the general hospital.
He was only six years old. His father was dead. His mother was sick and could not take care of him. So he had to be brought to the hospital in Edinburgh.
One day my friend, Rev. George Wilson, went in and sat by the bed of the suffering little boy.
He was telling him that the doctor was coming on Thursday to take off his little leg.

You parents can imagine it. Suppose one of your children, six years old, was far from home in a hospital. Suppose he was told that the doctor was coming on a certain day to take off his leg. Think how he would suffer at the thought!
Of course, the little boy was very upset about it.
The minister asked about his mother. She was sick, and his father was dead.
The minister wanted to comfort him, so he said, “The nurse is such a good woman. She will help you.”
“Yes,” said the boy, “and maybe Jesus will be with me.”
Do you have any doubt about that?
The next Friday the man of God went to the hospital, but he found the bed empty.
The poor boy was gone. The Savior had come and taken him into His arms.
In our great cities, aren’t there hundreds and thousands of people who need human sympathy in some way?
That will speak to their hearts much more loudly than eloquent sermons.
Many people who won’t be moved by eloquent sermons would give in to tenderness, gentleness, and sympathy.
The great Dr. Chalmers said, “The little I have seen of the world, and what I know of human history, teaches me to look at people’s mistakes with sorrow, not with anger.

I take one poor heart that has sinned and suffered. I picture the struggles and temptations it has been through. I think of its brief moments of joy, its tears of regret, its weak resolve, and the scorn of a world that has little kindness. I think of the ruin of the soul’s inner sanctuary and the threatening voices inside. Its health is gone, its happiness is gone. When I think of all this, I would gladly leave the wandering soul of my fellow man with Him, from whose hands it came.”
Some of you may say, “How can I come to feel real sympathy for people who are grieving?”
That is a very important question.
Many people work for God, but they seem to do it in such a professional way.
I will tell you how you can learn to feel sympathy.
I have found this rule very helpful.
Put yourself in the place of the grieving and suffering people you want to show sympathy to.
If you do that, you will soon win their hearts and be able to help them.
A few years ago God taught me a lesson I will never forget.
I was superintendent of a Sunday school in Chicago with more than 1,500 students.
In July and August many of the children died. Most of the ministers were out of town, so I had to go to a great many funerals.
Sometimes I had to go to four or five in one day.
I got so used to it that I did it almost like a machine.
I could watch a mother take her last look at her child and see the lid of the coffin closed, and not be moved at all.
One day when I came home, my wife told me that one of the Sunday school children had drowned. The mother wanted to see me.
I took my little daughter with me, and we went to the house.
I found the father drunk in one corner of the room.
The mother told me that she took in other people’s washing to earn a living for herself and her children, because her husband drank away all his wages.
Little Adelaide used to go to the river and collect floating wood for the fire.
That day she had gone as usual. She saw a piece of wood a little way out from the bank. As she stretched out to reach it, she slipped, fell into the water, and drowned.
The mother told me her sad story. She had no money to buy a burial cloth and a coffin, and she wanted me to help her.
I took out my notebook and wrote down her name and address. I also took the measurements for the coffin so I could send them to the undertakers.
The poor mother was very upset, but it didn’t seem to move me.
I told her I would be at the funeral, and then I left.

As my little girl walked beside me, she said, “Papa, suppose we were very poor, and Mama had to wash clothes to earn a living. And suppose I had to go to the river to get sticks for the fire. If I fell into the water and drowned, would you feel bad?”
“Feel bad! Why, my child, I don’t know what I would do.
You are my only daughter. If you were taken from me, I think it would break my heart.”
And I hugged her close and kissed her.
“Then did you feel bad for that mother?”
That question cut me to the heart!
I went back to the house, took out my Bible, and read the fourteenth chapter of John to the mother.
Then I prayed with her and tried to comfort her.
When the day of the funeral came, I went.
I hadn’t been to the cemetery for many years. It was several miles away, and I had thought my time was too valuable.
I found the father still drunk.
I had gotten a plot for little Adelaide in the strangers’ field.
As we were putting the coffin into the grave, another funeral procession arrived. That body was going to be buried nearby.
As we were covering the coffin, Adelaide’s mother said, “Mr. Moody, it is very hard to bury her among strangers.
I have moved around a lot and have lived among strangers. I have never had a burial plot.
It is so hard to put my firstborn among strangers.”
I said to myself that it would be very hard to have to bury my own child in the strangers’ field.
By now I fully shared the poor mother’s feelings.
The next Sunday I told the children in the Sunday school what had happened.
I suggested that we buy a Sunday school burial plot. Then when any of the children in the school died, they would not be buried in the strangers’ field. They would be put in our own plot.
Before we could get the deed drawn up, a mother came and asked if her little girl, who had just died, could be buried in the plot.
I told her I would give permission.
I went to the funeral. As we were lowering the little coffin, I asked what the child’s name was.
She said it was Emma.
That was my own little girl’s name. I couldn’t help crying as I thought how I would feel if it were my own Emma.
Do you think I couldn’t sympathize with that grieving mother?
Very soon after that, another mother came and wanted her dead child buried in our plot.
She told me his name was Willie.
At that time that was the name of my only son. I thought how I would feel if it were my Willie who had died.
So the first children buried there had the names of my two children.
I tried to put myself in the place of these grieving mothers. Then it was easy for me to share their grief and point them to the One who “will wipe away all tears from their eyes.”
Nine years ago, when I came back to Chicago, one of the first things I did was drive out to see our children’s plot.
I had thought it would last many years, but it was nearly full. Many of my old Sunday school students had died while I was away. Their bodies were resting in this plot until the great day.
But I learned that the children of the Sunday school were about to buy another, larger plot. Under normal circumstances it would be enough for many years.
Many little ones are buried there, waiting for the resurrection. I would like to be buried beside them. It would be so sweet to be with them when we rise and meet our Lord.
Dear friends, if you want to fully share the feelings of others, put yourself in their place.
May God fill our hearts with the spirit of the good Samaritan, so that we will be full of tenderness and love and compassion.
I want to give you a motto that has helped me a great deal.
It was a Quaker’s motto:
“I expect to pass through this world only once.
So if there is any kindness I can show, or any good thing I can do for any fellow human being, let me do it now. Let me not put it off or neglect it, for I will not pass this way again.”
“Don’t be fooled: God will not be made a fool of. Whatever a person sows, that is what he will also reap.
The one who sows to his flesh will reap ruin and decay from the flesh. But the one who sows to the Spirit will reap everlasting life from the Spirit.”
Galatians 6:7–8.
I think this passage holds truths that no unbeliever or doubter will dare to deny.
Some passages in God’s Word need no other proof. We can easily find the proof in what we see every day.
This is one of those passages.
Suppose the Bible were wiped out of existence. The words I have just quoted would still be proved true, over and over, by what is always happening around us.
All we have to do is pick up the daily newspaper. There we can see these words coming true before our eyes.
I remember once announcing this text, and a man stood right up in the crowd and said:
“I don’t believe it.”
I said, “My friend, that doesn’t change the facts.
Truth is truth whether you believe it or not. And a lie is a lie whether you believe it or not.”
He didn’t want to believe it.
When the meeting ended, a police officer was waiting at the door to arrest him.
He was put on trial for stealing and sent to prison for twelve months.
I really believe that once he was locked in his cell, he believed that he had to reap what he had sown.
Trying to wipe this truth out of God’s Word would be like trying to wipe the sun out of the sky.
It is a law that heaven has made, and it lasts forever.
This law has been in force for six thousand years.
Didn’t God make Adam reap what he had sown, even before he left the Garden of Eden?
Didn’t Cain have to reap outside of Eden?
It may be a king on his throne, like David, or a priest at the altar, like Eli. It may be a priest or a prophet, a preacher or a listener. Every person must reap what he sows.
I believed this ten years ago. But today I believe it a hundred times more.
My text is true for each single person—whether he is a saint, a sinner, or a hypocrite who thinks he is a saint. It is true for families. It is true for society. It is true for nations.

I say this law is as true for nations as it is for single people: the results of what we do must be reaped. In fact, someone has said that nations do not go on living after this world ends. So this present world is the only place where they can be punished as nations.
Look at how God has dealt with them.
See if they have not reaped what they sowed.

Take Amalek. The Bible says: “Remember what Amalek did to you on the road when you came out of Egypt. He met you on the way and attacked the people at the back—all the weak ones lagging behind—while you were tired and worn out. He did not fear God.”
What would come of this attack?
Would it go unpunished?
God decided that Amalek would reap what they had sown. Under King Saul, that nation was almost completely wiped out.
What has happened to the kingdoms and empires of the world?
What brought Babylon to ruin?
Her king and her people would not obey God, and so ruin came on them.
What has happened to Greece and all her power?
Once she ruled the world.
What has happened to Rome and all her greatness?
When their cup of wickedness was full, it was smashed to the ground.
What has happened to the Jews?
They turned down salvation. They mistreated God’s messengers. They crucified their Redeemer. And we find that 1,100,000 of them died at one time.
Look at the history of our own country.
Our ancestors had the Bible open in front of them, and yet they planted slavery here. But in the end, judgment came.
There was not a family in the North or the South that did not have to grieve for someone taken from them.
Take France as an example.
People say that a hundred years ago, men in France were spending millions every year printing and handing out books and papers that attacked faith in God.
What has the harvest been?
Hasn’t France reaped what it sowed?
Look at the result: “The Bible was banned.
God was denied. All hell broke loose.
Half the children born in Paris were born to parents who were not married.
Between September 1792 and December 1795, more than a million people were beheaded, shot, drowned, abused, and put to death.
Since then, France has had thirteen revolutions in eighty years. And under the republic, the government has been overthrown on average once every nine months.

One out of every three babies born in Paris is born outside of marriage. In a single year, ten thousand newborn babies were pulled out of the water where the city sewers empty. The number of native-born French people is shrinking. More people take their own lives in Paris than in any other city in the Christian world. And since the French Revolution, so many French men and women have been killed in the streets of Paris in uprisings that it averages more than 2,500 people every year!”
This principle was not new in the Bible or in history when Paul explained it in his letter to the Galatians.

Paul describes it with words from the farm. But the Law of Sowing and Reaping shows up under other names too: the Law of Cause and Effect, the Law of Payback or Getting Even, and the Law of Compensation.
I don’t plan to get into a discussion of the philosophy of this law, under any of these names, right now.
We can see that it exists.
No reasonable person can argue with it.
Doubters may pick at and criticize many other things in the Bible, but they have to admit that this is true.
It does not need the Bible to back it up. Thinkers agree about it as much as they agree about anything.
Someone may object, though. He may say that this law may work in the physical world, but it is not so sure in the spiritual world.
This is exactly where modern research comes in.
Researchers have found that the laws of the spiritual world are mostly the same laws that work in the natural world.
In fact, some claim that the spiritual world came first and the natural world came after. They say that when God set out to make the universe, He followed patterns that were already laid down.
In short, they say God brought the higher laws down into the natural world. So the natural world became “the supernatural in bodily form, a picture you can see, a working model of it.”
“In the spiritual world, the same wheels turn—only without the iron.”

So our whole life is surrounded and ruled by laws that God has set up. One of those laws is that a person reaps what he sows. This law is easy to see and to test, whether we are talking about sowing to the flesh or sowing to the Spirit.
Sin brings a bad harvest. Doing right brings a good harvest. Each one follows the sowing as surely as a crop of wheat or barley does.
“Life is not a matter of chance. It is a matter of cause and effect.”
As we go on, we will see that this law was at work in the very earliest times of Bible history.
Job’s three friends decided that he must be a terrible sinner. They took it for granted that the disasters that hit him had to be the result of his wickedness.
One of them said, “Think about it, please: has an innocent person ever been destroyed? When have good people ever been wiped out?
From what I have seen, those who plow evil and sow wickedness reap the same thing.”
In the book of Proverbs it says: “Wicked people do work that cheats. But whoever sows what is right will get a reward that is sure.”
And again: “Whoever sows evil will reap nothing but emptiness.”
In Isaiah we find these words: “Tell good people that things will go well for them. They will enjoy the fruit of what they have done.
But how terrible for the wicked! Things will go badly for them. They will be paid back for what their hands have done.”
Hosea warned Israel: “They have sown the wind, and they will reap the whirlwind.”
He advised them: “Sow for yourselves by doing what is right, and reap a harvest of mercy.”
The Bible is full of comparisons taken from nature.
When Christ was on earth, His favorite way to teach was to take truths about heaven and dress them in everyday, earthly pictures.
One writer put it like this: “Truths came from His lips. He did not simply state them and ask people to take His word for it. He based them on the patterns of the universe.
His human mind was in perfect harmony with God’s mind, to which it was joined. So He could see how things are connected. He could read God’s eternal will in the simplest laws of nature.

For example, suppose the question was whether God would give His Spirit to those who asked. He did not answer with a truth that people had to accept on His word alone. He took the answer from facts that anyone could see for himself.
‘Look at the birds in the sky’; ‘look at the lilies in the field’—learn from them the answer to your question.
There was a principle in it.
God meets the needs that He Himself has created.
He feeds the ravens. He clothes the lilies. And He will feed the hungry spirits of His children with His Spirit.”
This is the kind of teaching Paul uses in our text.
He takes the simple work of sowing and reaping, which everyone knows, and finds in it a deep spiritual and moral meaning.
It is as if he were saying that every person, as he travels through life, is scattering seed with every step.
The seed is his thoughts, his words, and his actions.
They leave him. Then, sooner or later, they spring up and bear fruit, and the time for reaping comes.

blocks.x: Life Is a Time for Sowing

s: This comparison teaches us some serious lessons.
We should see life as a time for sowing.
Everyone has his own field to sow, to take care of, and in the end to reap.
We are growing the seed for the coming harvest by our habits, by the time we spend with friends and companions, and by letting good or bad influences into our lives.
We cannot watch the seed as it grows and develops, but time will show it.
The whole harvest is already hidden inside the seed. In the same way, the full results of sin or of holiness are already hidden inside a sinful act or a holy act.
“When wrong desire has become pregnant, it gives birth to sin. And when sin is fully grown, it gives birth to death.”
We cannot reap a good harvest unless we have sown good seed. In the same way, we cannot reap eternal life unless we have sown to the Spirit.
Weeds are easy to grow.
They grow without anyone planting them.
And sin springs up naturally in the human heart.
Ever since our first parents broke away from God, the human heart, left to itself, has been completely rotten. Everything it has produced has been evil.
“People’s hearts are completely set on doing evil.”
Do you doubt it?
If you do, ask yourself what would happen to a child left on its own—with no training, no guidance, and no schooling.
Even with all that is done for children, evil too often wins out.
Good seed has to be planted and looked after, often with hard work and trouble. But the harvest will be sure.
Do we want other people to love us when we go through hard times?
Then we must love them when they most need that love to cheer them up.
Do we long for people to care about us when we are sad or hurting?
Then we will have it, if we have also cried with those who cry.
Are we hoping to reap eternal life?
Then we must not sow to the flesh, or we will reap ruin and decay. We must sow to the Spirit. Then we have the promise that we will reap its fruit that never dies.
Dr. Chalmers has pointed out the difference between sowing and reaping.
“Notice this,” he says. “Giving in to the desires of the flesh is one thing. Setting things up so that you can give in to them is another.

Suppose a man is suddenly provoked, and he takes out his angry feelings on the neighbor who has offended him. At that moment he is not getting ready to satisfy a sinful feeling. He is actually satisfying it.
At that moment he is not sowing. He is reaping a harvest of pleasure, such as it is.
This difference can help us judge how ungodly certain kinds of people are.
Think of the drifting pleasure-seeker who is swept along by every impulse. His self-control has become so weak that he is a slave to every urge. He lives in a never-ending harvest of sinful pleasure.

Or think of a daughter whose only joy is to rush from one expensive, glittering party to the next. She pushes away every worry and fills every hour with the silly fun and charms of her restless crowd. Nothing could be more opposite to a life spent getting ready for the coming judgment or for eternity.
And yet she is reaping, not sowing.
Someone else has the job of earning the money that buys everything. She simply enjoys what the money buys.
It is the father who sows.

He is the one who sits, busy and brooding and anxious, over his business deals. Worry may have given him wrinkles. The years have sobered him until he has no taste at all for the glitter and emptiness of fashionable society.”
The father sows, and he reaps in the life of his daughter.
There was a famous painter who was well known for how carefully he did his work.
When someone asked him why he took so much trouble, he answered:
“Because I am painting for eternity.”
It is a serious thing to think that the future will be the harvest of the present—that how things stand with me when I die may depend on what I do today!
When we believe in life after death and in a coming judgment, the present becomes much more important.
Things that last forever depend on it.
The chance to sow will not last forever. It is slipping through our fingers moment by moment. And the future can only show the harvest of the seed we sow now.
Once a sculptor showed a visitor around his studio.
It was full of statues of gods.
One of them was very strange.
Its face was hidden, covered with hair, and it had wings on each foot.
“What is his name?” the visitor asked.
“Opportunity,” the sculptor answered.
“Why is his face hidden?”
“Because people seldom recognize him when he comes to them.”
“Why does he have wings on his feet?”
“Because he is soon gone. And once he is gone, no one can ever catch him.”
So we should make the most of the opportunities God has given us.
What our future will be depends a great deal on us.
We can sow for a good harvest. Or we can act like the Sioux Indians once did. The United States Commissioner of Indian Affairs sent them a supply of grain to plant, and they ate it.
People keep giving up their eternal future for a moment of fun right now. They fail, or they don’t bother, to see that the future depends on the present.

blocks.x: Nothing Is Too Small to Matter

s: From this we can learn that nothing on earth is too small to matter.

Every thought, every word, and every act has an influence that lasts forever. Each one will come back to us, just as seed comes back as a harvest. When we understand this, we must see how much responsibility they carry, however small they may seem.
We easily overlook the results that depend on small things.
The idea of the law of gravity came from an apple falling.
People say that some years ago a Harvard professor brought some gypsy moths to this country. He hoped they could be usefully crossbred with silkworms.
By accident, the moths got loose. They multiplied so much that the state of Massachusetts has had to spend hundreds of thousands of dollars trying to get rid of them.

H. M. Stanley once pushed his way through the forests of Darkest Africa. The most dangerous enemies he met there were the little Wambutti dwarfs. They killed more people in his caravan than anyone else, and they came closest to wrecking his whole expedition.
They caused so much trouble that he could only move very slowly through the areas where they lived.

These little men had only little bows and little arrows that looked like children’s toys. But on those tiny arrows was a small drop of poison. It could kill an elephant or a man as fast and as surely as a Winchester rifle.
They defended themselves with poison and traps.
They would sneak through the dark forest, hide and wait, and shoot their deadly arrows before anyone could spot them.
They dug ditches and carefully covered them with leaves.
They stuck spikes in the ground, put the deadliest poison on the tips, and then covered them up.
People and animals would fall into these ditches or step on these spikes and die.

A woman was once writing to a young man in the navy whom she hardly knew. She thought, “Should I end this letter the way anyone would, or should I say a word for my Master?” She quietly prayed for a moment. Then she wrote to him that his constant moving from place to place was a good picture of the verse, “Here we have no city that lasts.” And she asked whether he could say, “I am looking for the one that is coming.”
Nervously she folded the letter and sent it.
An answer came back.
“Thank you so much for those kind words!
I am an orphan. No one has spoken to me like that since my mother died, many years ago.”
That arrow was shot without knowing where it would land, but it hit its target. Soon afterward the young man was rejoicing in the full blessing of the gospel of peace.
One Sunday an unknown man preached to a few people in a Methodist chapel in the south of England.
A fifteen-year-old boy was in the crowd. A snowstorm had driven him into the chapel.
The man took as his text the words, “Look to me and be saved.” As he stumbled along as best he could, the light of heaven flashed into that boy’s heart.
The boy left the chapel saved. Soon he became known as C. H. Spurgeon, the boy preacher.
One night the pastor’s house at Epworth, England, caught fire. Everyone inside was rescued except one son.
The boy came to a window. Two farm workers brought him safely to the ground, one standing on the other’s shoulders.
That boy was John Wesley.
Do you want to understand how much that event mattered? Do you want to measure what came from that rescue? Ask the millions of Methodists who look back to John Wesley as the founder of their church.

chapters.title: Don’t Be Fooled: No One Makes a Fool of God

s: “Don’t let anyone fool you.”—Ephesians 5:6.
“Will you mock Him the way one person mocks another?”—Job 13:9.
We have all lived long enough to know what it is like to be fooled.
We have been fooled by our friends and by our enemies, by our neighbors and by our relatives.
Ungodly companions have fooled us.
At every turn in life, someone has taken advantage of us in one way or another.
False teachers have crossed our path. They pretended to be helping us, but they poisoned our minds with wrong ideas.
They gave us hopes that turned out to be false. Those hopes were like the apples of Sodom: pretty on the outside, but full of ashes inside.

They told us there is no God, no life after death, and no judgment coming. Or they said that everyone will be saved, that there is plenty of time to repent, or that we can be saved by doing the best we can.
Sin has fooled us.
Every sinner believes something that is not true.
Sin comes to him with a smile. It offers him pleasures and delights that are not pure and do not last.
During our meetings in Boston, a young man came into the Tabernacle.
He looked around and thought to himself that the people who came there were big fools—people who had businesses, nice homes, and good clothes.
He had nothing in the world. He was a homeless drifter, and he went in there just to keep warm.
He could not understand why people who had homes would come and spend their time listening to the kind of stuff I preached.
One night, after he had been coming for two weeks, I happened to point right down to where he was sitting. I said, “Young man, don’t be fooled!”
God used those words like an arrow.
He began to think about his own life.
He remembered the time when he had a good job in Boston. Back then he was a young man earning good pay. He moved in good society and had lots of friends.
Then he looked at the state he was in now.
His friends were all gone. His clothes were gone. His money was gone. And there he was, an outcast in that city.
He said to himself, “I have been fooled.” That very hour, God woke him up.

He wanted to get friends to pray for him. But he could not afford to buy a piece of paper or pay for a stamp. So he found an old, dirty scrap of paper, stood in the street, and wrote a request to be read in the Tabernacle. It said that if God would save a poor, lost man like him, he wanted to be saved.
That prayer was answered.
Just as it happened to Nebuchadnezzar, his friends gathered around him again. The Lord gave him back his position and his place in society.
His eyes were opened, and he saw how he had been fooled.
How many people all over the world are being fooled by the god of this world!
People have said that in the recent war between France and Germany, German drummers and trumpeters used to play French drum signals and bugle calls to trick their enemies.
It is said that the Germans often gave the orders “Halt!” or “Stop firing!” So the French soldiers were led into places where they could be shot down like cattle.
Satan is the chief enemy of our souls. He has often blinded our thinking and tricked our conscience with his lies.
He has often come looking like an angel of light, hiding his ugliness under a borrowed cloak.
He says to a young man, “Go ahead and sow your wild oats.
There is plenty of time to get religious when you are old.”

The young man gives himself over to a life of wild spending and excess. He falsely hopes that he will find real satisfaction. It is a good thing if he wakes up to the trick before his desires become his masters and drag him down into deep need and misery.
Satan promises his victims great things if they give in to their desires, but those promises never come true.
The pleasure he promised turns out to be pain. The heaven he promised turns out to be hell.
Be careful that Satan does not fool you the way he fooled Eve in the beginning.
“There is no truth in him.
When he tells a lie, he is speaking from his own nature, for he is a liar, and lies come from him.”
But most of all, we have been fooled by our own heart.
Who has not found out that this Scripture is true: “The heart is more deceitful than anything else, and it is terribly wicked. Who can understand it?”
“How many times have we said we would never do a certain thing again, and then done it within twenty-four hours!
A person may think he has reached the bottom of his heart. But he finds there are deeper places he has not reached.
What terrible self-deception comes from it!
Solomon said, “Anyone who trusts his own heart is a fool.”
Luther once said that he was more afraid of his own heart than of the Pope and all the cardinals.
Many wives have come to me in tears about their husbands. They say, “He is good at heart.”
The truth is, that is the worst spot in him.
If the heart were good, everything else would be right.
Everything in our life flows out of the heart.

Christ said: “From inside, out of people’s hearts, come evil thoughts, adultery, sexual sin, murder, stealing, greed, wickedness, lying, shameless lust, jealousy, speaking evil against God, pride, and foolishness.”
That is what Christ Himself said about the heart that has not been made new.
Some years ago an unusual painting was shown in London.
When you looked at it from far away, you seemed to see a monk praying, with his hands folded and his head bowed.
But when you came closer and looked more carefully, you saw that he was really squeezing a lemon into a bowl of punch!
What a picture of the human heart!

If you look at it only on the surface, you think the heart is the home of everything good and noble and pleasing in a person. But really, until the Holy Spirit makes it new, it is the home of everything rotten.
“This is the reason people are condemned: the light has come into the world, and people chose darkness over light.”
A Jewish rabbi once asked his students what was the best thing a person could have to keep him on the right path.
One said a good nature. Another said a good friend. Another said wisdom was the best thing he could wish for.
Finally one student answered that he thought a good heart was best of all.
“That’s right,” said the rabbi. “You have included everything the others said.
A person who has a good heart will have a good nature, will be a good friend, and will be wise.
So let everyone always grow a heart that is sincere and honest. It will save him from a great deal of sorrow.”
We need to pray David’s prayer: “Create a clean heart in me, O God, and make my spirit right again inside me!”
Remember this: the God of the Bible has never deceived anyone. He cannot, and He never will. That is the difference between the God of the Bible and the god of this world.
He sees how people live. He looks into their hearts. He knows their secret ways. They don’t need to tell Him anything, and they cannot hide anything from Him.
We may be very good at fooling ourselves and others, or at being fooled by them. But we cannot fool Him.
Adam and Eve tried it in Eden. They hid from Jehovah among the trees of the garden.
Saul tried it. He kept the best sheep and cattle of the Amalekites alive and pretended that he was going to sacrifice them to God.
Ananias and Sapphira tried it. They secretly kept back part of the money from the land they sold.
“Why did you let Satan fill your heart so that you lied to (tried to fool) the Holy Spirit? … You were not lying to people, but to God.”
People try it every day.
They have gotten the idea into their heads that God can be fooled.
They can fool their pastor, their boss, and their friends, so they think they can fool God too.
They put on a false front. They use empty words. They go through the motions of serving God without meaning it. They make lame excuses. They practice every kind of hypocrisy.
But it does no good.
No one can trick God.
He sees the rot inside the tomb that is painted white on the outside.
Notice that Paul gave this warning to Christians—to the believers in the church in Galatia.
After all, a person is not fooled all the time about the more obvious, shameful sins.
In his sober moments, the drunkard knows where a life of heavy drinking must end.

He loses his self-respect and the respect of his friends. Soon his body starts to show the marks—shaky hands and a blotchy face. These things are the quick harvest of drunkenness, and they are easy to spot as they ripen.
The man who lives a sexually immoral life also reaps the early fruit of his sin in diseases of the body. These are often strong warnings to stop going down such a dangerous road.
But it is different with “respectable” sins.
A person may be sowing them for years and not even know it himself.
You remember that in the story of the farmer sowing seed, some seeds fell among thorns. The thorns grew up and choked them.

When our Master explained this story, He said: “The one who received the seed among the thorns is the person who hears the word. But worry about this world and the false promises of riches choke the word, and he produces no crop.”
Who would have expected the world or riches to do that?
But someone has said that Christ never spoke about riches except to warn people.
Today we don’t tend to see riches that way.
People are trampling on one another in their chase for money.
“Don’t be fooled.” Whoever sets his heart on money is sowing to the flesh, and from the flesh he will reap ruin and decay.
“Hard times have killed thousands, but good times have killed tens of thousands.”
Two gentlemen were walking past a fine mansion surrounded by beautiful, rich fields. One asked the other, “What is this estate worth?”
“I don’t know what it is worth. But I know what it cost the man who owned it until he died.”
“How much?”
“His soul.”
An English minister was called to the bedside of a rich member of his church who was dying.
The pastor knelt beside the dying man and asked him to hold his hand while he prayed for God to hold him up in that serious hour. But the man would not give his hand.
After he died, they pulled back the covers. His stiff hands were found clutching the key to his safe in a death grip.
Right to the end, his heart and his hand held on to his possessions. But he could not take them with him.
A person may be proud, and people may even call his sin a virtue.
Listen to what God’s Word says: “Proud eyes and an arrogant heart are sin”; and “The Lord hates everyone whose heart is proud.”
These are the mistakes people make.
They live respectable lives, and they think everything is fine.
They do not see that rot has spread into many of the things their hearts love most.
Most of all, people who call themselves Christians need to be careful that they are not being fooled.
How carefully people should watch their thoughts, their habits, and their feelings!
Most of the time, people are fooled because they neglect things.
They do not stop to examine themselves. They do not open up their hearts and minds as if they stood before God, and judge themselves by His perfectly holy will.
A man does not have to shoot himself to kill himself. He only has to stop eating properly, and he will soon die.
When an enemy is strong and on the attack, an army is sure to be beaten and captured unless it keeps a sharp lookout, with every soldier wide awake at his post.
People have noticed that there are more accidents in Switzerland in good weather than in stormy weather.
In good weather, people tend to set out on trips they would not try in worse conditions, and they are less careful about what they do.
In the same way, moral and spiritual disaster usually hits people when they are off guard and careless about temptation.
When life is going well, they become proud and depend on themselves. But hard times drive them to the living God for guidance and comfort.
Dr. Johnson once said that there is so much falsehood in the world more because people are careless about the truth than because they tell lies on purpose.
That is why we must keep watch all the time.

The Persians had a festival once a year when they killed all the snakes and poisonous creatures they could find. But then they let them multiply as fast and freely as ever until the festival came around again.
That was a foolish plan.
Sins are like snakes. They multiply quickly, and we need to watch for them all the time.
And we should keep watch on every side.
Many people have fallen at the very place where they thought they were safest.
Moses was so gentle and humble that people still talk about it.
Yet he lost the Promised Land. He let the people of Israel provoke him, and “he spoke carelessly with his lips.”
Peter was the most eager and daring of the disciples, bold and outspoken. Yet for a short time he sank into being a lying, cursing, sneaking coward who was afraid of a servant girl.

There is an old fable about a deer with only one eye who used to graze near the sea. To stay safe, she kept her blind eye toward the water, since she did not expect any danger from that side. With her good eye she watched the land.
Some men noticed this. They took a boat, came at her from the sea, and shot her.
With her last breath she said:
“Oh, what a cruel fate! I got my death wound from the side where I expected no harm, and I was safe on the side where I looked for the most danger.”
Let danger and need drive you closer to God.
He never dozes or sleeps. When He is keeping you, you will be safe.
Hold on tight to Him in prayer.
“Watch and pray.”
Christianity is not to blame for the deceit found among people who claim to follow it.
Someone has used this example before: blaming Christianity would make as much sense as blaming the Cunard shipping company when a passenger jumps off one of their ships at sea and kills himself.
If that person had stayed on the ship, he would have been safe. And if the disciple had stayed true to what he believed, he would never have turned out to be a hypocrite.
Was anyone ever harsher in speaking against hypocrisy than Christ?
Do you want to know why, every now and then, the church is shocked when some leading church member or Sunday school leader is exposed?
It is not his Christianity that caused it. It is his lack of it.
Some secret sin has been eating away at the heart of the tree. Then, at a critical moment, the wind blows it down, and everyone sees how rotten it was.
The deception cannot possibly last forever.
Lincoln used to say that you may be able to fool all the people some of the time, and some of the people all the time, but you will not be able to fool all the people all the time.
If the deception has not been found out sooner, death will uncover it. And the poor victim will stand, no longer fooled, before a God who cannot be mocked.

chapters.title: When You Sow, You Expect to Reap

s: “Look at the farmer. He waits for the precious crop to come up from the ground. He is very patient with it, until the early and late rains come.”—James 5:7.

Notice these four things about sowing and reaping. When someone sows, he expects to reap. He expects to reap the same kind of seed that he sows. He expects to reap more than he sowed. And not knowing what kind of seed it is makes no difference.
First: When someone sows, he expects to reap.
Imagine a farmer who kept sowing, spring after spring, but never harvested anything in the fall. You would say he belonged in a mental hospital.
No, he is always looking ahead to the time when he will reap the reward for his hard work.
He never expects the seed he has sown to be lost.
A young man spends a long time as an apprentice, learning some trade or profession. But he expects that someday he will reap the fruit of all those years of patient hard work.
Ask an engineer why he works so hard for five, six, or seven years trying to learn his profession.
He answers that he is looking forward to the reaping time, when he will make his fortune and his name.
The lawyer studies long and hard. But he too is looking forward to the time when he will have many clients and be paid back for all his work.
Many medical students have a hard time supporting themselves while they are in college.
As soon as they get their diplomas and become doctors, they expect the reaping time to come. That is what they have been working for.
Some crops ripen almost right away. But as a rule in the natural world, it takes time before the seed is fully grown.
Still, it is growing the whole time. First the little green shoot breaks through the soil. Then comes the stalk, then the head of grain, and then the head full of ripe grain.
The farmer is not disappointed when his crops do not all pop up overnight like mushrooms.
He waits patiently, knowing that the reaping time will come at the right season.
It is the same with the harvest of what we do.
Few people, if any, would give in to sin unless they expected to get some pleasure from it.
A drunkard does not drink just for the sake of drinking. He drinks because he hopes to enjoy himself right now.
A thief does not steal just for the sake of stealing. He steals to get something out of it.
And it is the same with a good person.
He does not make sacrifices just for the sake of sacrificing. He makes them because he hopes and expects that by doing so he will do good and help others.
All these things are ways of reaching a goal. There is always the hope of a harvest.
The text tells us to look ahead to the certainty of reaping: “Whatever a person sows, that is what he will also reap.”
We know what it is like when crops fail. But in the spiritual world, the harvest can never fail.
Wet soil can rot the seed. Frost can kill the early buds. The weather can be too wet or too dry for the crops to ripen. But none of these things can stop the harvest of what a person does.
The Bible tells us that God will pay back every person for what he has done.

“Some people patiently go on doing what is right. They are seeking glory and honor and a life that cannot die. To them God gives eternal life. But some people are quarrelsome. They do not obey the truth; they obey what is wrong. For them there will be anger and fury. Trouble and deep pain will come on every person who does evil.”
So we should be very careful about everything we do—with our bodies, in our morals, and with our minds!
The things we do, the words we say, and the thoughts we hold on to are all written down. Each one will get the reward it deserves, because God does not treat one person better than another.
We must not miss this: the harvest has to come. It is the natural result of the sowing.
People have said that God is not some kind of moral tyrant, even though many people often think of Him that way.
He does not sit on a throne handing out a penalty for each action as it comes before Him to be judged.
Instead, He has set up certain laws. The law of sowing and reaping is one of them. Punishment is simply the natural result of sin.
There is no way out.
You have to bear it. Other people may have to reap alongside you, but no one can reap in your place.
The text also teaches that the harvest is always one of two kinds.
This law leads in two directions, and only two. If you sow to the flesh, you will harvest ruin and decay. If you sow to the Spirit, you will harvest everlasting life.
“Sowing to the flesh” does not just mean taking good care of your body.
The body was made in God’s image. The body of a believer is a temple of the Holy Spirit. We can be sure that God is pleased when we take good care of that image.

No, the phrase means giving in to the body’s cravings and spoiling it. It means feeding its wrong desires while the higher part of a person suffers. It means indulging our animal urges, which become sinful when we go too far with them.
“Sowing to the flesh” means scattering seeds of selfishness. Those seeds always grow into a harvest of ruin.
“When we lived by the flesh, the pull of sin was busy in our bodies, making fruit that ended in death.”
And what does Paul say the flesh produces?

“Adultery, sexual sin, dirty living, shameless lust, worshiping idols, witchcraft, hatred, quarrels, jealousy, fits of rage, fighting, rebellion, taking sides, envy, murder, drunkenness, rowdy partying, and things like that.”
In 1867 I was at the big exhibition in Paris. There I noticed a small oil painting, only about a foot square. The face in it was the ugliest I have ever seen.
A paper attached to the painting said, “Sowing the Weeds.” The face looked more like a demon’s than a man’s.
As the man sowed these weeds, snakes and reptiles came up out of the ground and crawled up his body. All around him were woods, with wolves and other animals prowling in them.
I have seen that picture many times since then.
Oh! The time of reaping is coming.
If you sow to the flesh, you will reap what the flesh produces.
If you sow the wind, you will reap the whirlwind.
But don’t think that the only way to sow to the flesh is to give in to the worst, crudest sins.
Every desire and every action that is not aimed at God is seed sown to the flesh.
Suppose a man is sowing so he can harvest money or get ahead in the world. He is sowing to the flesh. He will reap ruin just as surely as the liar and the adulterer will.
The seed may look “polite” and “refined” and “respectable.” It may look very much like good seed. But what it really is will show in the end. The disease of decay will be on it.
With this judgment coming, how foolish it is for people to struggle so hard for these things!
Many people will give up their time, their health—even their good character—for money.
What do they get?
Ruin. They get something that does not last forever, something that has nothing of “everlasting life” in it.
John said, “The world will pass away, and so will the things people long for in it.”
Peter said, “Every human being is like grass. All human glory is like the blossom on the grass.
The grass dries up, and the blossom drops off.”
None of these earthly, fleshly things have roots in what lasts forever.
You may even see them disappear before your own short life is over.
People make this mistake. They sow to the flesh and expect to reap a spiritual harvest. Or they sow to the spirit and then feel let down when they do not get an earthly reward.
A teacher had been telling his class the story Jesus told about the rich man and Lazarus. Then he asked a question:
“Now, boys, which one would you rather be—the rich man or Lazarus?”
One boy answered, “I would rather be the rich man while I’m alive, and Lazarus when I die.”
That cannot happen. It is either the flesh and ruin, or the Spirit and everlasting life.
There is no bridge from one to the other.
“Seed sown for a spiritual harvest does nothing at all to bring earthly comfort and success.

Christ said, ‘Blessed are the pure in heart, because they will see God. Blessed are those who are hungry and thirsty for righteousness, because they will be filled’ (with righteousness). ‘Blessed are those who mourn, because they will be comforted.’
Notice what is promised: they will see the Almighty, they will be full of righteousness, and they will receive God’s comfort.
Nothing here is earthly. These are spiritual rewards for spiritual work.

It does not say that the pure in heart will become rich. It does not say that those who hunger and thirst for righteousness will be filled with bread. It does not say that those who mourn will move up in the world and become famous.
Each area of life has its own harvest. And that harvest comes only from its own kind of sowing.
“Everything reaps its own harvest. Every act has its own reward.
So before you envy what someone else enjoys, first work out what it cost him to get it.

“Take this example. A shopkeeper who follows God complains that his honesty holds back his business. Customers flood through the doors of his less honest neighbor on the same street. Meanwhile he sits for hours with nothing to do.
My brother, do you really think God is going to reward honor, integrity, and a noble heart with this world’s money?
Do you imagine He will pay you for spiritual goodness by sending you lots of customers?
Now think about the price that other man has paid for his success.
Maybe he has cheapened his mind and lost his honor on the inside.
All his ads are lies. He treats his workers like a tyrant. His prices are low only because his goods are poor.
If you sow that man’s seed, you will reap that man’s harvest.
Cheat, lie, say whatever it takes, and customers will come to you.
But if that price is too high, let him have his harvest, and you take yours. Yours is a clear conscience, a pure mind, and an honest life inside and out.
Would you trade that for his harvest?”
“Sowing to the Spirit” means saying no to yourself and fighting against evil. It means obeying the Spirit, walking in the Spirit, living in the Spirit, and being led by the Spirit.
We sow to the Spirit when we use our talents and our money to move spiritual things forward. We also do it when we support and encourage people who are spreading the Spirit’s influence.
We sow to the Spirit when we nail the flesh and all its cravings to the cross. We do it when we give ourselves to Him the way we once gave ourselves to the flesh.
A Jewish rabbi once said, “Every person has two drives inside: one good and one evil.
The person who gives God his evil drives offers Him the best sacrifice.”
The fruit of this kind of sowing is “love, joy, peace, patience, gentleness, goodness, faith, humility, and self-control.”
In this world, the harvest is a stronger character, more respect, and being more and more useful to others. In the next world, the harvest is being accepted by God and having everlasting life.

Henry Lloyd Garrison gave public speeches in England. Among the last words he is recorded to have spoken there were these: “I began speaking out against slavery in the Northern States of America while people threw bricks and rotten eggs at me. And I ended it in South Carolina, almost literally buried under the wreaths of flowers that the freed slaves of that state piled on me.”
During the Civil War, a young man worked for a large trading company in New York City. His job was to bargain with a certain man to buy a load of damaged beans.
The beans were bought and delivered. Then they were spread out on the top floor of the company’s building.
Workers were hired to turn the beans over and over and sprinkle them with soda water. This made them look better and easier to sell.

Then the company bought a large load of top-quality beans. First they put some good beans into the bottom of the barrels. Then they filled the barrels almost to the top with the poor beans. After that they put good beans on top again and sealed the barrels to sell.
The boss labeled the barrels “Beans—A1.”
The clerk saw this and said, “Sir, do you think it is right to label those beans A1?”
The boss snapped back, “Are you the head of this company?”
The clerk said nothing more.
The filling and sealing of barrels went on.
When everything was ready, the beans were put up for sale. There were many hundreds of barrels.
In the office, buyers were shown samples of the best beans.

At last a sharp buyer came in. (No one is so clever in business that he won’t often meet someone just as clever.) He looked at the samples in the office and asked the price. Then he wanted to see the whole stock.
The clerk was ordered to take the buyer up to the top floor and show him the stock.
He was shown an open barrel. It seemed to be the same quality as the sample.
Then the buyer said to the clerk:
“Young man, the bean samples you showed me are top quality. Nowhere in the market can anyone buy beans like that for the price you are asking. Something is wrong here.
Tell me, are these beans the same quality all the way down the barrel as they are on top?”
Now the clerk was in a hard spot.
He thought, “Should I lie for my boss? He clearly wants me to. Or should I tell the truth, no matter what happens?”
He chose the truth and said:
“No, sir, they are not.”
“Then,” said the customer,
“I don’t want them.” And he left.
The clerk went back into the office.
His boss asked him, “Did you sell that man those beans?”
He said, “No, sir.”
“Why not?”
“Well, sir, the man asked me if the beans were the same quality all the way down the barrel as they were on top.
I told him they were not.
Then he said, ‘I don’t want them,’ and left.”
“Go to the cashier,” said the boss, “and collect your pay. We don’t want you here anymore.”
The clerk got his pay and left the office. He was glad that he had not lied to serve someone’s dirty greed or to help a boss who had no principles.
Three weeks later the company sent for the young clerk. They begged him to come back and work for them again. They offered him three hundred dollars a year more than they had ever paid him before.
That is how his honesty and truthfulness were rewarded.
The company knew deep down that he had been right, even though it seemed they had lost a lot of money because of his honesty.
They wanted him back because they knew they could trust him. They knew he would never let them be hurt by cheating and lies.
They knew their money would be safe in his hands.
They respected and honored that young man.
Let us learn to be patient.
“Look at the farmer. He waits for the precious crop to come up from the ground. He is patient with it for a long time, until the early rains and the late rains come.”
A delay does not mean a “no.”
Too often one generation sows and the next one has to reap.
God is a jealous God. He brings “the sins of the fathers on their children, down to the third and fourth generation of those who hate Him.”
In the early years, when Israel first became a nation of its own, God commanded them to let the land of Canaan rest every seventh year.

“For six years you are to plant your land and gather its crops. But in the seventh year you must let it rest and leave it alone. Then the poor among your people can eat from it, and the wild animals can eat what they leave.
Do the same with your vineyard and your olive trees.”
From the time Saul was anointed king, the people did not keep this law.
After four hundred and ninety years, God let the nation be taken captive for seventy years.
During that time the land got its rest. It had seventy Sabbath years to make up for all the Sabbath years it had missed.
Those Israelites sowed the bitter seed of disobedience. Their children and grandchildren had to reap the harvest in exile and captivity.
One day a leading surgeon did a dangerous operation in front of his students.
As far as his part went, the operation was a success.
But he turned to the class and said, “Six years ago, living wisely might have prevented this disease.
Two years ago, a safe and simple operation might have cured it.
Today we have done our best with the case as it is now. But Nature will have her say.
She does not always cancel her death sentences.”
The next day the patient died. He was reaping the fruit of his wild, unhealthy living.
Paul says, “Let us not grow weary of doing what is right. When the time comes, we will gather the crop—as long as we do not quit.”
Not long ago Mr. Edison was talking with a reporter. Without even meaning to, he preached a very powerful sermon about sticking with it and being patient.

He described how he tried again and again to make the phonograph play back a certain breathy sound. Then he added, “For the last seven months I have worked eighteen to twenty hours a day on this one word: ‘specia.’
I said into the phonograph, ‘specia, specia, specia,’ but the machine answered, ‘pecia, pecia, pecia.’
It was enough to drive a person crazy!
But I didn’t give up, and I have succeeded.”
When Daniel Webster was a young lawyer in Portsmouth, someone brought him an insurance case.
Only a small amount of money was at stake. All he was promised was a twenty-dollar fee.
He saw that to do his very best for his client, he really should travel to Boston to study in the law library there.
The trip would cost him more than he earned. And he would not be properly paid for his time.
But he made up his mind to do his best, whatever it cost.
So he went to Boston, looked up the past cases and laws, and won the case.
Years later, Webster had become famous. One day he was passing through New York.
An important insurance case was going to trial that day, and one of the lawyers had suddenly become sick.
Money was no problem, so they begged Webster to name his price and take the case.
“I told them,” said Mr. Webster, “that it was ridiculous to expect me to prepare a legal argument with only a few hours’ notice.
But they kept insisting that I at least look at the papers. Finally I agreed.
It was my old twenty-dollar case all over again! And since I never forget anything, I had all the past cases and laws right at my fingertips.
The court knew I had had no time to prepare. They were amazed at how much I knew.
So you see, that trip to Boston paid me back richly, in fame and in money. And the lesson is this: good work is rewarded in the end.”
Two men were digging for gold in California.
They worked very hard and found nothing.
Finally one of them threw down his tools and said:
“I’m leaving before we starve.” And he left.
The very next day his partner’s patience paid off. He found a gold nugget that kept him going until he made a fortune.
“People see that punishment for evil does not come right away. So their hearts are fully set on doing evil.

A sinner may do wrong a hundred times over and have his life stretched out. Even so, I am sure of this: it will be well for those who fear God and show Him reverence. But it will not be well for the wicked. He will not stretch out his days; they are like a shadow, because he does not fear God.”
Some people think that if they do something in the dark, it will never come to light. That idea is deadly. God says it will be brought to light.
A man who has hidden his sins is foolish to think they will never rise up again or that there will be no final judgment.
Look at Jacob’s sons.
They sold their brother Joseph and lied to their father.
Twenty long years went by. But their sin followed them all the way down to Egypt. There they said, “We are guilty of our brother’s blood.”
At last the time of reaping had come for those ten boys who sold their brother.
Once, when I was preaching in Chicago, a woman came to me who was nearly out of her mind.
You know, some people make fun of religious meetings. They say religion drives people crazy.
But it is sin that drives people crazy.
It is not having Christ that sinks people into despair.
Here was the woman’s story. She had a family of children.
One of her neighbors had died, and her husband brought home a little child.
She said, “I don’t want this child.” But her husband said, “You must take it and look after it.”
She said she had enough work with her own children. She told her husband to take that child away.
But he refused.
She admitted that she tried to starve the child, but it kept on living.
One night it cried all night long. I suppose it was hungry.
At last she took the bedcovers, threw them over the child, and smothered it.
No one saw her. No one knew anything about it.
The child was buried.
Years went by. Then she said, “I hear that child’s voice day and night.
It has driven me nearly crazy.”
No one saw what she did. But God saw it, and this punishment followed.
History is full of things like this.
You don’t even have to go to the Bible to find it out.

chapters.title: You Expect to Reap the Same Kind You Sow

s: “Plants that make seeds, each of its own kind, and trees that bear fruit . . . each of its own kind.”—Genesis 1:12.
“Can grapes be picked from thorns? Can figs be picked from thistles?”—Matthew 7:16.
“If you live to please the flesh, you will die. But if the Spirit helps you kill off the wrong things your body does, you will live.”—Romans 8:13.
Suppose I told you that I planted ten acres of wheat last year and watermelons came up. Or suppose I said I planted cucumbers and picked turnips. You wouldn’t believe me.
It is a fixed law: you reap the same kind of seed you sow.
Plant wheat, and you get wheat. Plant an acorn, and an oak comes up. Plant a little elm, and in time you have a big elm.
Lukman was a storyteller from the East who told fables. One day his master said to him, “Go to that field and sow barley.”
But Lukman sowed oats instead.
At harvest time his master went to the field. He saw green oats coming up, and he asked Lukman:
“Didn’t I tell you to sow barley here?
So why did you sow oats?”
Lukman answered, “I sowed oats hoping that barley would come up.”
His master said, “What a foolish idea!
Have you ever heard of such a thing?”
Lukman answered, “You yourself keep sowing seeds of evil in the field of this world. Yet you expect to reap the fruits of goodness on the day of resurrection.
So I thought maybe I could get barley by sowing oats, too.”
The master was ashamed at this answer, and he set Lukman free.
In plants, like produces like. In work, like produces like too.
If a man has learned to be a carpenter, he doesn’t expect to be an excellent watchmaker.
If he has worked hard to learn the law, he doesn’t expect to earn his living as a doctor.
People expect to reap in the same line of work they have learned.
This law is just as true in God’s kingdom as in human kingdoms. It is just as true in the spiritual world as in the natural world.
If I sow weeds, I will reap weeds. If I sow a lie, I will reap lies. If I sow adultery,
I will reap adulterers. If I sow whisky, I will reap drunkards.
You cannot erase this law. It is in force.
No other truth in the Bible is more serious.
Suppose a neighbor I don’t want to see comes to my house. And suppose I tell my son to say I am out of town if the neighbor asks for me.
My son goes to the door and lies to my neighbor. Before six months are up, that boy will be lying to me. I will reap that lie.
Some time ago a man asked me, “Why can’t we find honest clerks these days?”
I answered, “I don’t know. But maybe I can guess why.

Merchants teach their clerks to say that cloth is all wool when it is half cotton. They mix cheap stuff into groceries and call them pure. They grind up white marble and mix it into powdered sugar. And the clerk knows about it. When that happens, you won’t have honest clerks.”
Merchants teach their clerks to lie and to mislead. They put a French or English label on goods made at home and sell them as imported goods. As long as they do that, they will have dishonest clerks.
Dishonest shop owners produce dishonest clerks.
I am not telling you made-up stories. I am telling you the truth.
This is not poetry. It is plain, serious fact: a person must reap the same kind of seed he sows.
This is a huge argument against selling alcohol.
Leave aside the questions of temperance and religion. Even so, no man on earth can afford to sell strong drink.
If I sell liquor to your son and turn him into a drunkard, someone will sell liquor to my son and turn him into a drunkard.
Every man who sells liquor has a son or a brother or some other relative who is a drunkard.
Where are the sons of liquor dealers?
Who have their daughters married?
Look around. See if you can find a man who has been in that business for twenty years who does not have a dark secret in his own family.

I made that challenge once. The next day a man said to me, “I wasn’t at your meeting last night. But I hear you made the shocking claim that no man has been in the liquor business twenty years without the curse coming into his own family.”
“Yes,” I said, “I did.”
“It isn’t true,” he said, “and I want you to take it back.
My father sold liquor, and I sell liquor, and the curse has never come into my father’s family or into mine.”
I said, “What? Two generations selling that hellish stuff, and the curse has never come into the family?
I will look into it. If I find I was wrong, I will take it back just as publicly as I said it.”
Two well-known men from the town were in the room. While the man was talking, I noticed a strange look on their faces.
After he left, one of them said:
“Mr. Moody, did you know that man’s own brother was a drunkard? He killed himself a few weeks ago. He left a widow and seven children, and they are living in that man’s house right now!
And he himself was a terrible drunkard until the shock of his brother’s suicide cured him.”
I don’t know how to explain what he said, unless he thought his brother wasn’t a relative.
Maybe he was like Cain, who said, “Am I my brother’s keeper?”
When I was the pastor of a church in Chicago, we were trying to reach the working men.
They used to say to me:
“Come down to the factory at lunchtime, and we’ll give you a chance to speak.”
I would ask them, “Why won’t you come to the church?”
“Oh,” they would say, “in church you get to do all the talking, and we can’t answer back. But come to the factory, and we’ll ask you a few questions.”
So I went down there, and sometimes they gave me a really hard time.
One of their favorite people to bring up was Jacob.
Many times men said to me, “You think Jacob was a saint, don’t you?
He was a big crook.”
Many said they thought Jacob wasn’t as good as Esau.
Notice this. In the Bible you read, “I will punish Jacob for what he has done.”

This law of payback runs all through his life. He was a friend of God, a relative of Abraham, and third in the family line of God’s covenant. Still, God made Jacob reap the same kind of seed he had sown.
Someone has said that “Jacob’s troubles were always the kind that brought his own wrongs back to his mind—both the picture of them and the punishment for them.”

When Isaac was old, he wanted some wild game to eat, and he sent Esau out to hunt it. But Jacob slipped out and took a young goat from his father’s flock. His mother Rebekah cooked it. Then Jacob brought it to his old, blind father and said he was Esau.
The old man recognized Jacob’s voice. But Jacob had cleverly put the goatskin on his hands and neck. So the old man felt him and said:
“The voice is Jacob’s voice, but the hands are Esau’s hands.”
With this lie he got the blessing that belonged to his brother as the firstborn. But he paid ten thousand times more for it than it was worth.
“Whoever steals my purse steals trash.”
The man who steals my wallet is the one who suffers most, not me. When Jacob grew old, he was always suspicious that his sons were deceiving him.
The sin of deceiving his own father produced its fruit.
Jacob was the big loser in this deal.
When Esau came back, Jacob had to run for his life.
Then God met him at Bethel.

“And look! The Lord stood above it and said, I am the Lord, the God of your father Abraham and the God of Isaac. I will give the land you are lying on to you and to your children after you. They will be as many as the specks of dust on the ground. You will spread out to the west and to the east, to the north and to the south. Every family on earth will be blessed in you and in your children after you.
“Remember, I am with you. I will watch over you in every place you go, and I will bring you home to this land. I will not leave you until I have done all that I told you.”
People read that far in Jacob’s life and say, “I don’t want anything more to do with a God who shows kindness to a man who did something so low.”
My friend, wait a minute.
Follow him to Padanaram.
He stayed there twenty years. During that time his pay was changed ten times.
He worked seven years to marry the lovely Rachel. Then he was tricked into marrying another woman.
Jacob had used a trick to get the blessing that belonged to the firstborn son. But Laban mockingly reminded him, “In my country we don’t give the younger daughter before the firstborn.”
He found out that Laban could drive just as hard a bargain as he could.
Wherever you find a sharp, tricky man, you will always find that he attracts men just like himself. And the one who cheats will be cheated himself.
“Birds of a feather flock together.” People who curse God end up together, and sharp, tricky men end up together.
In Laban, Jacob found a man just like himself.
It was one sharp diamond cutting another.
Look a little further.
Jacob had twelve sons. But he loved Joseph and Benjamin more than the others, because they were the sons of Rachel, the wife he loved.
He favored Joseph and had a coat of many colors made for him.
Playing favorites will bring out the old sinful nature in any family.
One morning Joseph, with an innocent heart, told a dream. In the dream his father and all his brothers bowed down to him.
Then his brothers began to plot how to get rid of him. His father sent him to find them while they were taking care of the flocks. When they saw him, they said:
“Now he’s in our hands! Let’s kill him and toss his body into a pit. Then we’ll say some wild beast devoured him.”

Later they sold him. They took his coat of many colors and dipped it in the blood of a young goat. They brought it to their father and said, “We found this. Look at it—is it your son’s coat or not?” He recognized it and said, “It is my son’s coat. A vicious animal has devoured him.”
Now notice this. Jacob tricked his father with the skin of a young goat. And his sons tricked him with the blood of a young goat.
Jacob lied to his father, and his sons lied to him.
The lie came back home.
Every lie will surely come back to you.
You can’t dig a grave so deep that what you bury will not rise again.
Tramp, tramp—your sins will all come back.
“Make no mistake: your sin will catch up with you.”
You may think you are very clever and can see far ahead. You may think you can plan and cover things up. But heaven above has decided that no sin will stay covered. God will uncover it.
You cannot fool the Almighty.
Jacob found that out.
He had to reap what he sowed.
Now look at David.
Some years ago a man said to me:
“Don’t you think David sank as low as Saul?”
Yes, he fell even lower, because God had raised him higher.
Here is the difference. When Saul fell, he showed no sign of being sorry. But when David fell, a cry of grief rose from his broken heart. He truly repented.
No one in the whole Bible rose so high and fell so low as David.
God took him from caring for sheep and put him on the throne.
He gave him plenty of riches and land.
David stood at the very top of glory. People loved and honored him.

But one day, you remember, David was walking on the roof of the palace. He saw Bathsheba, and he lusted after her, and he committed the terrible sin of adultery. Then, to cover up that sin, he got Bathsheba’s husband drunk and had him murdered.
Then God’s sentence came: “I will stir up trouble in your own family, and the sword will never leave your house.”
David’s son Amnon commits adultery with David’s own daughter.
Absalom throws a feast for Amnon and has him murdered.

Not long after, Absalom comes with an army to drive his father David off the throne. On the roof of the palace he openly commits adultery with David’s concubines. If God had not been in control, Absalom would have killed his father.
David sowed adultery, and he reaped it in his own family.
He sowed murder, and he reaped it in his own family.
I believe I know what brought that bitter cry from the father’s heart when he said, “Oh, my son Absalom, my son, my son Absalom!
I wish I had died for you!” It was the fact that this was the payment for his own sin.
From the time he fell into that sin with Uriah’s wife until the day he was buried, one wave of trouble after another rolled over him.
God did not spare David. So if we fall into sin and do not confess it and turn away from it, do you think He will spare us?
If ever a man had the chance to cover up his sins, it was David.
No judge or jury dared to condemn him.
It was done in secret, but his sin caught up with him.
Nathan was sent to cross his path. And, young man, a Nathan will show up for you someday too.
If you do not repent and turn from your sins, some messenger will stop you in your tracks.

My friend, why not call on God right now, as David did when he came to his senses? Pray the same prayer he prayed. How thankful we should be that we have that prayer! Why not pray it on your knees right now?

blocks.x: David Asks God to Forgive Him

s: “O God, show me mercy, because your love is kind. Your tender mercies are so many—so wipe out the wrongs I have done.
Scrub away every bit of my guilt, and make me clean from my sin.
I know the wrongs I have done. My sin is always in front of me.
I have sinned against you—only you. I have done this evil right in front of you. So you are right when you speak, and fair when you judge.
Look, I was shaped in sin from the start. My mother conceived me in sin.
Look, you want truth deep inside a person. In the secret places of my heart, you will teach me wisdom.
Make me pure with hyssop, and I will be clean. Wash me, and I will be whiter than snow.
Let me hear joy and gladness. Let the bones you have broken be glad again.
Turn your face away from my sins. Wipe out all the wrong I have done.
Make a clean heart in me, O God. Give me a new and right spirit inside.
Don’t send me away from you, and don’t take back your Holy Spirit.
Give me back the joy of being saved by you. Hold me up by your Spirit, who gives freely.
Then I will show wrongdoers how you want them to live, and sinners will come back to you.
O God, the God who saves me, rescue me from the guilt of shedding blood. Then I will sing out loud about your righteousness.
Lord, open my lips, and I will speak out your praise.
You are not asking for animal sacrifices—if you were, I would give them. Burnt offerings do not make you glad.
What God wants as a sacrifice is a spirit that is broken. A heart that is broken and crushed with sorrow, O God, you will never look down on.”
But you say you don’t believe the Bible.
Then look at history, and see whether this law is true.
Maxentine built a fake bridge to drown Constantine, but he was the one who drowned.
Bajazet meant an iron cage for Tamerlane. But Tamerlane carried Bajazet around in that very cage.
Maximinus put out the eyes of thousands of Christians. Soon afterward a terrible eye disease broke out among his people, and he himself died of it in great pain.
Valens had about eighty Christians put on a ship, sent out to sea, and burned alive. Later he was beaten by the Goths and ran away to a cottage, where he was burned alive.
Alexander VI was poisoned by wine he had prepared for someone else.
Henry III of France was stabbed in the same room where he had helped plan the cruel massacre of French Protestants.
Marie Antoinette was riding to Notre Dame Cathedral for her wedding. She told the soldiers to order all the beggars, the crippled, and the people in rags to get away from the route of the parade.
She could not stand to look at these poor, miserable people.
Not long after, she was tied up in the executioner’s cart, riding to the place where she would be put to death. Crowds stared at her with hearts as cold as ice and as hard as granite.
When Foulon was asked how the starving people were supposed to live, he said, “Let them eat grass.”
Later, a furious mob caught him in the streets of Paris. They hanged him, stuck his head on a pike, and stuffed his mouth with grass.

chapters.title: You Reap More Than You Sow

s: “But some seed landed on good ground and gave a harvest—some a hundred times what was sown, some sixty times, some thirty times.”—Matthew 13:8.
If I sow one bushel of seed, I expect to reap ten or twenty bushels.
In one day I can sow what it will take ten men to reap.
The Spanish have a saying: “Sow a thought, and you reap an act.
Sow an act, and you reap a habit.
Sow a habit, and you reap a character.
Sow a character, and you reap a destiny.”
And reaping takes longer than sowing.
I have heard of a kind of bean that multiplies itself a thousand times.
People say that a single bit of thistle fluff blew off the deck of a ship and covered a whole South Sea island with thistles.
The oak grows from an acorn. The mighty Mississippi River starts from a little spring.
One glass of whisky can lead to dying as a drunkard.
One lie can ruin a person’s career.
One mistake made when you are young can follow you all your life.
Someone has said that many Christians spend half their time trying to keep down the sprouts of seeds they sowed when they were young.
If it is not kept under control, the wish to “have a drink” will grow into a thirst that eats you up. The wish to “play a game of cards” will grow into a gambler’s passion you cannot resist.
Abraham gave up his only son when God asked him to. As the fruit of that act of obedience, God gave him more descendants than the stars in the sky or the grains of sand on the seashore.
Jacob told one lie. Later his ten sons came back to him with a lie ten times as big.
For twenty years Jacob grieved over Joseph, because he thought Joseph was dead.
I am sure he cried for Joseph night after night. In his dreams he must have seen the boy torn to pieces and heard him crying for help.
It took him a long time to gather that harvest.
The people of Israel grumbled against God because of the report the spies brought back about the land of Canaan.
And didn’t they have to reap a harvest many times bigger?
