Listen: “You explored the land for forty days. So you will carry the punishment for your sins for forty years—one year for each day. Then you will know what it means when I take back my promise.”
Once in a meeting I said that a man has to reap more than he sows. A man sitting in front of me hung his head and sobbed out loud.
After the meeting, a friend came up to him and said:
“What’s wrong?”
He pointed at me and said, “Every word that man said is true.
Four years ago I was a trusted clerk for a company in this city.
I have good reason to think that if I had kept going the way I started, I would be a partner in that company today.
But one night I was drunk in a bar, and I committed a crime. I was sent to prison. There I repented with deep sorrow.
Today I came back for the first time. I went to my old company, and they told me to get out.
I went to other businesses where I knew people, and they treated me the same way.
On the street I met men I used to know. Some of them used to have lower jobs than mine. I tipped my hat to them, but not one of them greeted me back.”
The man twisted his hands in pain and said, “It’s all true. Reaping takes much longer than sowing.”
Do you doubt it?
Ask your neighbor who has thrown away his good name, his reputation and his home through drinking. He has brought ruin on his family.
It takes a long time to build a good character. But you can ruin it in just one hour.
Some years ago a man died in the prison at Columbus. He had spent more than thirty years in his cell.
He was one of the millionaires of Ohio.
Fifty years earlier, people were trying to build a main railroad line from Chicago to New York. They wanted to lay the tracks through his farm near Cleveland.
He did not want the railroad to cut his farm in two, so the case went to court. The court appointed officials to pay him for the damage and to let the railroad be built.
One dark night, after the tracks were laid, a train was knocked off the rails, and several people were killed.
People suspected this man. He was put on trial, found guilty and sent to prison for life.
Soon the farm was cut up into lots for building in the city, and the man became a millionaire. But he never got any good out of it.
The prison chaplain told me that before the man died, he became a child of God.
Maybe it took him no more than an hour to put that blockage on the railroad tracks. But he spent over thirty years reaping what came from that one act!
In the history of France we read about a king who wanted a new tool for torturing his prisoners.
One of the king’s favorite men suggested building a cage. It would be too short to lie down in and too low to stand up in.
The king liked the idea. But the first person put into the cage was the very man who thought of it! He was kept in it for fourteen years.
It probably took him only a few minutes to suggest that cruel idea. But he spent fourteen long years reaping what he had sown.
If a man could do his reaping all by himself, it would not be so hard. But it is terrible when he makes others reap with him—his godly father, his mother who loves him, or his wife and children.
Doesn’t the drunkard force his wife and children to reap a bitter harvest?
Doesn’t the gambler make his relatives reap along with him?
Doesn’t the prostitute make her parents reap pain and shame?
Sin is such a bitter enemy!
May God help each of us to turn away from it right now!
When I hear a young man joking about “sowing his wild oats,” I don’t laugh.

I feel more like crying. I know he is going to make his gray-haired mother reap in tears. He will make his wife reap in shame. He will make his old father and his innocent children reap along with him.
In just ten, fifteen or twenty years, he will have to reap those wild oats. No one has ever sown them without having to reap them.
If you plant the wind, you will harvest a whirlwind.
We cannot control our influence on others.
If I plant thistles in my field, the wind will pick up the fluffy thistle seeds when they are ready. It will blow them over the fence, and my neighbors will have to reap thistles with me.
In the same way, my children or my neighbors may copy my example. Then my actions get repeated through them again and again, for good or for evil.
Think how many people have been ruined because of the sins of men like Jacob, David and Lot!

blocks.x:
Nothing but leaves! The Spirit is grieved
Over years of wasted life!
Over sins we enjoyed while our conscience slept,
Over vows and promises we did not keep,
And from years of struggle we harvest—
Nothing but leaves! Nothing but leaves!

Nothing but leaves! No bundles of grain
From life’s good, ripening field;
We sow our seeds, and look! Only weeds—
Words, empty words, instead of real deeds—
Then with hard work and pain we reap
Nothing but leaves! Nothing but leaves!

Nothing but leaves! Sad memory makes
No curtain to cover the past;
And as we walk our tired way,
And count each lost and wasted day,
We sadly find at last—
Nothing but leaves! Nothing but leaves!

Oh, who will meet the Master like this,
Bringing only dried-up leaves?
Oh, who will come to the Savior’s feet,
Before the fearful judgment seat,
And lay down, instead of golden grain,
Nothing but leaves! Nothing but leaves?
—L. E. Ackerman.

chapters.title: Not Knowing What You Sow Changes Nothing

s: “Don’t be surprised at this. The time is coming when everyone lying in the grave will hear his voice and come out. Those who did good will rise to life. Those who did evil will rise to be condemned.”—John 5:28–29.
Now notice this too: it makes no difference if you don’t know what kind of seed you are sowing.
If I think I am sowing good seed but it turns out to be bad, I will get a bad harvest. So I need to make sure what kind of seed I am sowing.
Imagine I meet a man who is sowing seed, and I say, “Hello, stranger! What are you planting?”
“Seed.”
“Seed of what kind?”
“I don’t know.”
“You don’t know if it’s good or bad?”
“No, I can’t tell. But it’s seed, and that’s all I care to know. So I’m sowing it.”
You would say he was completely crazy, wouldn’t you?
But he would not be half as crazy as the man who keeps sowing for this life and for eternity, and never asks himself what he is sowing or what the harvest will be.
Father, what seeds are you planting in your family?
Are you giving your children a good example to follow, or a bad one?
Do you spend so much time at the bar or the club that your children hardly know you? Or are you raising them for God and for what is right?
There is a story about a man who said he would not talk to his son about religion. He said the boy should make up his own mind when he grew up, without being influenced by his father.
One day the boy broke his arm. While the doctor was setting the bone, the boy cursed and swore the whole time.
“Ah,” said the doctor, “you were afraid to influence the boy toward what is right. But the devil wasn’t afraid to influence him at all.
He has led your son the opposite way.”
Imagine a father thinking he should just let his children run wild!
Left to itself, nature never grows anything but weeds.
One of Coleridge’s friends once objected to choosing what young people should be taught. He thought that would unfairly bias their minds.
Coleridge, who was a philosopher and a poet, invited him to see his garden. He took him to a spot where ugly weeds with no sweet smell had grown thick all over the flower beds and the paths.
“You can’t call that a garden!” said his friend.
“What?” said Coleridge. “Do you want me to be unfair to the ground by favoring roses and lilies?”
Haven’t you ever noticed that the mind and the heart work the same way?
If a child has nothing to do, Satan will soon lead him into trouble.
Someone must keep an eye on him.

The things that will help build his character must be chosen for him, and harmful things must be kept away. This takes hard work. It is like a farmer who carefully grows useful crops, but keeps fighting against weeds and every unhealthy plant.
A murderer was about to be put to death for his crime.
Talking about his wild and reckless life, he said:
“How could I have turned out any different? I was raised so badly.
I learned these things from the time I was young.
When I was only four, my mother poured whiskey down my throat just to see what I would do.”
On the morning he was put to death, his miserable mother said goodbye to her son. Her own influence had helped bring him to that shameful end.
Early one morning, after a light snowfall, a father left home for his office.
He turned around and saw his two-year-old son trying to step his tiny feet into his father’s big footprints.
The little boy shouted, “Keep going, Papa! I’m coming! I’m coming right in your footprints!”
The father picked the boy up, carried him back to his mother, and started off for his office again.
He usually stopped at a bar on the way to have a glass of liquor.
That morning, as he stood in the bar’s doorway, he seemed to hear a sweet little voice say, “Keep going, Papa! I’m coming! I’m coming right in your footprints!”
He stopped. He paused. He thought hard about what the future would bring.
“I can’t make any footprints that I would be ashamed or sorry to see my boy walk in,” he said firmly. And he turned away.
Father, mother, neighbor, are your footprints leading the right way?
Are they straight? Can you turn to anyone walking behind you and say, “Follow me, just as I follow Christ”?
Are you guiding the little ones safely to the Great Shepherd?
The best time to plant good seed is before Satan has scattered his weeds.
God has warned us and told us many times to do this.
“Look first for God’s kingdom and for what is right in his eyes.”
“Teach a child the way he ought to go.”
“Don’t stir your children up to anger. Instead, raise them with the Lord’s training and correction.”
If a farmer doesn’t plant in the spring, he can never get that lost chance back. Neither can you, if you waste yours.
Being young is a time for planting. If that time passes without good seed being planted, weeds will spring up and choke the soil.
It will take hard, painful work to pull them out.
An old preacher once said that when a good farmer sees a weed in his field, he has it pulled out.
If the weed is pulled early enough, the empty spot soon fills in, and the crop waves over the whole field.
But if it is left too long, a bare spot stays there.
It would have been better never to let the weed take root at all.
Young man, are you letting some secret sin take control of you and tie you up hand and foot?
That sin is growing. Every sin grows.
Some years ago I was speaking to five thousand children in Glasgow. I took a spool of thread and said to one of the biggest boys:
“Do you think I can tie you up with this thread?”
He thought that was funny and laughed.
I wrapped the thread around him a few times, and he snapped it with one quick jerk.
Then I wrapped the thread around him again and again, and after a while I said:
“Now get loose if you can.”
He couldn’t move his hands or his feet.
If you are a slave to some filthy habit, you must kill that habit, or it will kill you.
My friend, what kind of seed are you planting?
Think back over how you have lived this past year.
Have you been living a double life?
Have you been claiming to believe, without really having what you claim?
If there is anything you can’t stand, it is hypocrisy.
Are you telling me God doesn’t hate it too?
If your right eye makes you sin, decide that you will tear it out. If it is your right hand or right foot, cut it off.
Whatever the sin is, decide that you will beat it, and do it now, without waiting any longer.
My friend, what kind of seed are you planting? Good seed or bad seed?
There will be a harvest, and you will have to reap it, whether you want to or not.
Tell me, what do you do with your free time?
Do you tell dirty stories that make other people’s minds filthy, while your own mind gets filthy too?
Do you read things that fill your mind with impure thoughts?
What do you do on the Sabbath?
Do you go boating, fishing, hunting, or on day trips?
Do you think preachers are old-fashioned and out of touch, and that the Bible belongs back in the Dark Ages?
Tell me how you treat your parents, and I’ll tell you how your children will treat you.
A man was getting ready to send his old father away to the poorhouse. Then his little child came up and said:
“Papa, when you get old, will I have to take you to the poorhouse?”
Don’t you ever write letters home to your parents?
They gave you clothes and paid for your schooling. And now you spend your nights gambling?
You tell your friends who don’t care about God that your father forced religion down your throat when you were a boy.
I have no respect at all for a man who says that about his father or mother.
Maybe they made a mistake. But it was a mistake of the head, not of the heart.
If they got a telegram saying you were sick with smallpox, they would take the first train to be with you.
They would gladly take the disease into their own bodies and die in your place.
If you make fun of your father and mother and look down on them, you will have a hard harvest. You will reap it in terrible pain.
Sooner or later it will come.
There is an old saying:

blocks.x:
“God’s mills grind slowly,
But they grind everything very fine.”

s: The Lord Jesus said, “The way you measure out to others is the way it will be measured back to you.”
The last time I was in London, a man told me that England was better than America in one way.
I asked him how. He said:
“In England we respect our laws more than you do in America.
You don’t hang even half of your murderers. But here, every murderer is hanged if he can be proven guilty.”
I answered, “Neither country hangs its very worst murderers.
If my son wanted to murder me, I would rather he killed me all at once than took five years to do it.
Think of a young man who comes home late night after night. When his mother begs him to stop, he curses her, gray hair and all. He is killing her little by little. He is the worst kind of murderer.”
This is happening all over the country.
Maybe you are not guilty of a sin as dark and ugly as this. But I tell you, every sin grows. If you have sin in your heart, you can’t know where it will take you.
Nothing pulls a son away from his mother, or a husband away from his wife, the way sin does.
God’s grace holds people together, but sin rips them apart and drives them away from each other.
Come on, my friend, what kind of seed are you planting?
What will your harvest be like?
Will it be a dark, sad harvest? Or will you have a happy one?
If you think wheat will come up after you have planted weeds, you are badly mistaken.
If you think you can let your passions and lusts run wild and still have eternal life, you are being fooled.
For God says, “If you sow seed for your sinful nature, it will give you a harvest of rot and ruin. But if you sow for the Spirit, the Spirit will give you a harvest of life that never ends.”
I beg you to be careful about which path you choose.
A farmer is careful when he picks his seed.
He doesn’t want bad seed or cheap seed, because he knows it will give him a poor crop.
He looks for the best seed money can buy.
If you choose to sow for your sinful nature, you will get a rotten harvest.
One sinful act could put you in a grave with shame on your name.
Choosing is a very serious thing.
You can make this very moment the turning point of your life.
Once, when Pizarro was conquering Peru, his men threatened to leave him.
They gathered on the beach to get on the ships and sail home.
Pizarro pulled out his sword and drew a line in the sand from east to west.
Then he turned toward the south and said:
“Friends and comrades, on that side are hard work, hunger, having no clothes, soaking storms and death. On this side are comfort and pleasure.
Over there is Peru with all its riches. Here is Panama with its poverty.
Let each man choose the way a brave man of Castile should.
As for me, I am going south.”
Then he stepped across the line. One by one his men followed him. And the future of South America was decided.
Napoleon was once offered a job as an officer in the Turkish army’s artillery.
He said no. But if he had said yes, the history of Europe would have turned out differently.
Your choice about spiritual things decides your eternity.
On one side is Christ. On the other side is the world.
You have to choose between them.
Don’t try to grow both wheat and weeds.
Oh, choose Christ! Don’t do it halfway.
Give all of your heart to Him.
He died to set you free from the curse of sin. And He lives to save you from sin’s power over you.
“Nobody can work for two masters at once.”
You can’t belong to two kingdoms at the same time.

Lord Brougham came to love the French town of Cannes so much that he tried to become a French citizen. But he found out he could not be both an English lord and a citizen of a French town. He had to give up one to become the other.
This is where your will comes in. It is easy to do what everyone else does, to go along with the crowd. But it takes character and moral backbone to stand against what most people think and do.
During the recent war, a soldier who had run away from his army came over to the Union lines near Pittsburg.
Someone asked him:
“Why did you join the side that broke away?”
He answered, “Because everybody else did.”
That reason explains why many people do what they do.
A man like that lives by the saying, “When you are in Rome, do what the Romans do.” He never bothers to find out whether the Romans are doing what is right.
If they are doing wrong, a man should stand up against a whole nation if he has to, like a new Daniel.
Almighty God put two choices in front of the people of Israel, and now I put them in front of you.
As you choose, remember that your eternity depends on it.

“Look! Today I am giving you a choice between life and good, or death and evil. I am commanding you today to love the Lord your God, to live the way He wants, and to obey His commands, His laws and His rules. Then you will live and grow in number, and the Lord your God will bless you in the land you are going to take for your own.

But if your heart turns away and you refuse to listen, and you are pulled away to worship other gods and serve them, then I warn you today: you will certainly be destroyed. You will not live long in the land you are crossing the Jordan River to take over.

Today I call heaven and earth to be witnesses against you. I have put in front of you life and death, blessing and curse. So CHOOSE LIFE, so that you and your children after you may live! Love the Lord your God, obey His voice, and hold on tight to Him. For He is your life, and He gives you long days to live.”
“You pay back each person for what he has done.”—Psalm 62:12.
“Every one of us will have to appear before Christ, the Judge. Each person will be paid back for what he did while living in his body, whether it was good or bad.”—2 Corinthians 5:10.
I can imagine someone saying, “I go to church, and I have heard that if we confess our sin, God will forgive us. But now I hear that I must reap the same kind of seed I planted.
How can both of these be true—that God forgives, and that God pays us back for what we do?
‘All of us have wandered off like sheep. Each of us has gone his own way. But the Lord put on him the guilt of all our sins.’
And yet you say I still have to reap what I have sown.”
Imagine I send my hired worker out to plant wheat.
When it grows up, there are thistles mixed in with the wheat.
A year ago there wasn’t a single thistle in that field.
I say to my worker:
“Do you know how these thistles got into the field?”
He says, “Yes, I do. You sent me to plant that wheat, but I was angry, so I mixed some thistle seeds in with it.
But you promised that if I ever did wrong and admitted it, you would forgive me. Now I’m holding you to that promise. I expect you to forgive me.”
“Yes,” I say, “you are right. I forgive you for planting the thistles. But here is what you must do: when harvest time comes, you must reap the thistles along with the wheat.”
Many Christians are reaping thistles along with their wheat.
Twenty years ago you planted thistles with your wheat, and now you are reaping them.
Maybe it was a dirty story. The memory of it keeps coming back to bother you, even at the most solemn moments.
Maybe it was something you said or did in a hurry that you have never been able to take back.
I heard John B. Gough say he would rather have cut off his own hand than have done a certain sin.
He didn’t say what it was, but I have always thought it was the way he treated his mother.
He was a miserable drunk lying in the gutter when his mother died. The poor woman couldn’t take it, and she died of a broken heart.
God had forgiven him, but he could never forgive himself.
Many people have done things they will never forgive themselves for, as long as they live.
Someone once said, “Right now, from the shameful graves of many prostitutes, a silent cry goes up for fair and just punishment.
From many a drunkard’s miserable home—from his heartbroken wife and his starving children—a terrible cry rises up into God’s ears.”
I believe God forgives sin completely and freely for the sake of Christ. But He lets some penalties stay.
If a man has wasted years in wild living, he can never get those years back to live them again.
If he has gone against his conscience, the scars will stay with him all his life.
If he has dirtied his good name, that stain can never be washed away.
If he ruins his body by giving in to his cravings and sins, he will suffer until he dies.
As Talmage says, “God’s grace gives you a new heart, but not a new body.”
“John,” a father said to his son, “please get me the hammer.”
“Yes, sir.”
“Now get a nail and a piece of pine board.”
“Here you go, sir.”
“Will you hammer the nail into the board?”
John did it.
“Now please pull it back out.”
“That’s easy, sir.”
“Now, John,” the father said in a quieter voice, “pull out the nail hole.”
Every wrong thing we do leaves a scar.
Even if the board were a living tree, the scar would still be there.
Even for our worst sins, there is rich and full redemption.
My sin can be made as white as snow and be gone completely, so that it can no longer disturb or spoil my friendship with God.

Yet even our smallest sins leave marks and results behind. They leave them in our lives, our characters, our memories and our consciences. Sometimes they leave us weaker. Often they affect our place in the world, our reputation, our success and our health. They leave their marks in a thousand ways.
God will not lift His little finger to take these away. He lets them stay.
No one should think that the Gospel, which announces forgiveness, can be turned into a cheap message that sin goes unpunished.
Not at all! Paul was talking to Christians when he said, ‘Don’t fool yourselves. No one can make a fool of God. Whatever you plant is what you will harvest.’
God loves us too much not to punish His children when they sin. And He loves us too much to wipe out (even if that were possible) the other results of our wrongdoing.

We must see both sides of the truth. First, the deepest and (as we call them) main penalties for our evil are swept away. These are being cut off from God and feeling the pain of our guilt. Second, other results are allowed to stay. And because God allows them, they can become a blessing and do good to the people who did wrong.

MacLaren says, “If you waste your youth, no amount of repenting will turn back the shadow on the sundial. It will not win back the ground you lost by being lazy. It will not bring back the health you wrecked by wild living. It will not return the strength and money you wasted on sin. It will not bring back the chances that slipped away.

All the wounds can be healed. For the Good Doctor—praise His name!—has knives and bandages, healing ointment and medicine for pain, even for the deadliest wounds. But scars remain even after the cut has closed.”
God forgave Moses and Aaron for their sins, but both of them still paid the penalty.
Neither of them was allowed to go into the promised land.
At the river crossing of Jabbok, Jacob became a “prince of God.” But for the rest of his life, his body carried the mark of that struggle.
Paul’s “thorn in the flesh” was not taken away, even after he prayed hard for it again and again.
But it lost its sting and became a way for him to receive God’s grace.
Maybe that is one reason God does not take away these penalties of sin.
He may mean for them to be signs that He is correcting us.
“The Lord corrects the people He loves.”
And if all the results of sin in this life were taken away, we would be likely to fall back into sin.
The penalty keeps reminding us how weak we are, and how much we need to be careful and to lean on God.
One night in Chicago, at the end of a meeting in the Y.M.C.A. rooms, a young man jumped to his feet and said, “Mr. Moody, may I say a few words?”
I said, “Of course.”
Then for about five minutes he begged those men to break free from sin. He said:
“If anyone cares about your soul, be kind to them. They are the best friends you have.
I was an only child, and my mother and father cared about me very much.
Every morning when the family prayed together, my father prayed for me. And every night he put me into God’s care.
I was wild and reckless, and I didn’t like the rules at home.
When my father died, my mother started leading the family prayers.
Many times she came to me and said, ‘Oh, my boy, if you would just stay for family prayers, I would be the happiest mother on earth. But when I pray, you won’t even stay in the house.’
Sometimes I came home at midnight after a night of wild partying and heard my mother praying for me.
Sometimes in the early hours of the morning I heard her voice begging God for me.
At last I felt I had to either become a Christian or leave home. So one day I packed a few things and sneaked away without telling my mother.
“Some time later I heard from someone else that my mother was sick.
Ah, I thought, it’s the way I’ve been acting that is making her sick!
My first thought was to go home and cheer her up in her last days. But then I thought that if I did, I would have to become a Christian.
My proud heart fought against it, and I said, ‘No, I will not become a Christian.’”
Months passed. At last he heard again that his mother was getting worse.
Then he thought:
“If my mother dies, I will never forgive myself.”
That thought brought him back home.
He got to his old village around dark and started walking toward the house, which was about a mile and a half away.
On the way he passed the graveyard. He decided to go to his father’s grave to see if there was a new grave next to it.
As he got close, his heart began to beat faster. When he was near enough, the moonlight showed a freshly dug grave.
Full of emotion, he said:
“Young men, for the first time in my life this question hit me: Who is going to pray for my lost soul now?
Father is gone, and Mother is gone. They are the only two people who ever cared about me.
That night, if I could have called my mother back and heard her whisper my name in prayer, I would have given the whole world—if it had been mine to give.
I spent the whole night by her grave. And for Christ’s sake God heard my mother’s prayers, and I became a child of God.
But I have never forgiven myself for the way I treated my mother, and I never will.”

blocks.x:
Where is my wandering boy tonight—
The boy I cared for so tenderly,
The boy who was once my joy and light,
The child I loved and prayed for?

Once he was as pure as the morning dew,
When he knelt by his mother’s knee;
No face was so bright, no heart so true,
And no one was as sweet as he.

Oh, if only I could see you now, my boy,
As lovely as in days gone by,
When your chatter and smiles made home a joy,
And life was like a happy song.

Go find my wandering boy tonight,
Go search for him anywhere you like;
But bring him to me with all his ruin and shame,
And tell him I love him still.

s: My dear friends, God may forgive you. But even if you are forgiven, the results of your sin are going to be bitter.
A few years ago I was preaching in Chicago on this Bible verse: “Get up, go to Bethel, and settle there.”
After the meeting, a man asked if he could talk to me alone.
I went into a room where we could be alone.
Drops of sweat stood on his forehead. I said:
“What’s wrong?”
He answered, “I am running from the law.
I am living far from home, in disguise.
My state’s government has offered a reward for catching me.
I’ve been hiding here for months.
People tell me there is no hell. But it feels like I have been in hell for months.”
He had been a businessman. He thought he had plenty of money, so he forged some bonds. He figured he could write a check any time and buy them back. But he got in over his head and was ruined.
He said, “I’ve been here six months.
I have a wife and three children, but I can’t write to them, and I can’t hear from them.”
The poor man was suffering terribly in his mind.
I said, “Why don’t you go back, turn yourself in, face the law, and ask God to forgive you?”
He said, “I would take the first train tomorrow and turn myself in, except for one thing.
I have a wife and three children. How can I bring this shame on them?”
I have a wife and three children too. When he said that, things looked very different to me.

Oh, if we could do our reaping by ourselves, it would not be so bitter. But when we make our little children, our dear wife, our old gray-haired mother or our old father reap with us, isn’t that reaping bitter?
I am not as afraid of any plague or sickness as I am of sin.
If God will just keep sin out of your family, I will praise Him in this life and forever.
Sin is the worst enemy a person could ever meet.
When someone comes to me for advice, I always try to put myself in that person’s place. Then I give the best advice I can.
So I told this man:
“I don’t know what to tell you, but it is safe to pray.”
After I prayed, I urged him to pray too. But he said:
“If I do, it means going to prison.”
I asked him to come back the next day at noon.
He met me right on time and said:
“It’s all decided. If I am ever going to meet the God of Bethel, I have to go through prison to meet Him. With God’s help, I will turn myself in.
I’m going back. Please keep this quiet until I have handed myself over to the law. After that, you can use my story as a warning.
When I started out in life, I never dreamed I would end up like this!
When I married a girl from one of the finest families in the state, I never dreamed I would bring such shame on her.”
At four o’clock that afternoon he headed back to Missouri.
He got home a little after midnight and spent a week with his family.
In a letter he said he didn’t dare let his children know he was there. He was afraid they would tell the neighbors’ children.
At night he would sneak out and look at his children. But he couldn’t hug them or kiss them.
Oh, that is what sin does!
How I pray to God that every one of us would turn away from sin today!
One day, while this man was hiding, he heard his little boy say:
“Mommy, doesn’t Daddy love us anymore?”
“Yes, he does,” his mother answered.
“Why are you asking?”
“Well,” the little boy said, “he’s been gone so long. He never writes us any letters, and he never comes to see us.”

On the last night he came out of hiding and took a long look at his innocent children as they slept. Then he held his wife and kissed her again and again. He left that once happy home and turned himself in to the sheriff.
The next morning he admitted he was guilty and was sent to prison for nineteen years.
I believe God had forgiven him. But he couldn’t forgive himself, and he had to reap what he had sown.
I begged the governor to show mercy, and the man was pardoned.
Some time ago I was telling this story, and someone didn’t believe it. But the governor who had pardoned the man happened to be at the meeting. He stood up and said, “I pardoned that man myself.”
The governor set him free, and he lived a few more years. But from the moment he committed that sin, he had to reap.
Oh, reader, I beg you: win the battle over the sin that keeps tripping you up, whatever it is.
I can imagine someone saying, “I’m glad Mr. Moody hasn’t tried to scare us about what happens after we die.
I agree with him that we get all our reward and punishment in this life.”
If you think I believe that, you are very wrong.
One sentence spoken by the Son of God about life after death has settled the question in my mind forever.
“If you die still in your sins, you cannot come where I am.”
If a man has not given up his drinking, his swearing, his sexual sin and his greed, heaven would be like hell to him.
Heaven is a place made ready for people who are made ready.
What would a man do in heaven if he can’t stand being around pure and holy people here on earth?
It is not true that we reap all our reward and punishment in this life.
Look at how many crimes are committed where the criminals are never caught.
Often the worst criminal uses his experience to avoid being found out, while someone more innocent gets caught.
A man leads a girl into sexual sin and ruins her life.
Is he always punished for it here on earth?
No. He holds his head as high as ever in society. Meanwhile the poor girl who was the victim of his lust—who perhaps was tricked into sin by him while she was innocent—becomes an outcast.
But his punishment has only been put off. At the very latest, it will come in the next world.

Oh, the clanging bells of Time!
Night and day they never stop;
We are tired of their ringing,
For they do not bring us peace.
And we hold our breath to listen,
And we strain our eyes to see
If your shores are coming near—
Eternity! Eternity!

Oh, the clanging bells of Time!
How their ringing rises and falls,
But deep beneath, grand and low,
Sounding clearly through it all,
Is a voice that must be heard,
As our moments rush away,
And it always says one word—
Eternity! Eternity!

Oh, the clanging bells of Time!
To their voices, loud and soft,
In a long line that never rests
We are marching back and forth;
And we long to see or hear
Something of the life to come,
For your breath is all around us—
Eternity! Eternity!

Oh, the clanging bells of Time!
Soon their sound will all be gone,
And in wonderful joy and peace
We will feel the silence come;
And our souls will quench their thirst,
And our eyes will see the King,
When your glorious morning dawns—
Eternity! Eternity!
—Ellen M. H. Gates

s: “Be careful that no one fools you.”—Matthew 24:4.
“Christ in you is the hope of glory. We preach Him. We warn everyone and teach everyone with all wisdom, so that we may present everyone perfect in Christ Jesus.”—Colossians 1:27–28.
Giving a warning is a sign of love.
Who warns like a mother? And who loves like a mother?
Perhaps your mother has died, and your father too.
Let me take the place of those who are gone, and raise my voice to warn you.
Like Paul, I would say: “I am not writing these things to shame you. I am warning you as my dear sons.”
A pilot was guiding a steamboat down the Cumberland River. In the middle of the narrow channel he saw a light. It seemed to come from a small boat.
His first thought was to ignore the signal and run the boat down.
As he came closer, a voice shouted: “Keep away! Keep away!”
He was very angry. He cursed the man, thinking it was a boatman who was in his way.

When he reached the next landing, he found out what had happened. A huge rock had fallen from the mountain into the riverbed. A signal had been put there to warn the boats coming down of a danger they did not know about.
Sadly, many people treat God’s warnings the same way. They get angry with anyone who tells them about the rocks in their path.
In the end they will understand better.
The people of Israel had no truer friend than Moses.
Whenever they went the wrong way, he warned them. And trouble only came to them when they ignored his warnings.
Elijah was the best friend Ahab had.
I wish I could warn people the way Jesus Christ did.

As He went up the Mount of Olives, His heart seemed deeply moved. He cried out, “O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you kill the prophets and stone the people sent to you! How often I wanted to gather your children together, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings. But you were not willing!”
Didn’t He warn them?
Suppose a friend of mine was about to put his money into a worthless silver mine. Would I be a true friend if I did not warn him?
And do I love him any less because I warn him not to do things that will bring a harvest of misery and despair?

“Suppose someone hears the trumpet but does not take the warning, and the sword comes and kills him. Then he is to blame for his own death. He heard the trumpet but did not take the warning, so his death is his own fault.
But whoever takes the warning will save his soul.”
Make sure that the seed you are sowing is good seed.
If you sow to the flesh, a good harvest is impossible.
If good seed and bad seed are allowed to grow together, they cannot both do well.
One grows at the cost of the other. And most likely the bad will win.
Weeds always seem to grow and spread faster than good seed.
The longer they live, the stronger the weeds’ hold becomes.

Waiting is dangerous. In the year 1691, a message was sent through the Highlands of Scotland. It said that everyone who had rebelled against the lawful government would be pardoned. But first, before the last day of the year, he had to lay down his weapons and promise to stop rebelling.
Many did this. But one chief named Maclan kept putting it off from week to week. He always meant to give in before it was too late.
When at last he set out to accept the pardon, a great storm held him back. He did not arrive until the time was up.
The day of pardon was over, and the day of punishment had come. Maclan and his men were put to death.
So it is wise to get rid of the weeds right away.
And be careful not to stay in sin any longer.
The deeper you sink, the more painful it will be to be restored.
Why keep deadening your conscience and sowing the seeds of even sharper regret?
No matter how much it hurts, break with sin right now.
Serious operations are often needed. A skilled surgeon knows that the disease cannot be cured by treating only the surface.
The farmer takes his hoe, his spade, and his axe. He cuts away the harmful plants and burns the roots out of the ground with fire.
If your right eye causes you to sin, pull it out and throw it away. It is better for you if one part of you is lost than if your whole body is thrown into hell.
And if your right hand causes you to sin, cut it off and throw it away. It is better for you if one part of you is lost than if your whole body is thrown into hell.
Remember that the weeds and the wheat will be separated on Judgment Day, if not sooner.
Sowing to the flesh and sowing to the Spirit always lead down different paths.
The axe will be put to the root of the trees. Every tree that does not produce good fruit will be chopped down and thrown into the fire.
The threshing floor will be cleaned completely. The wheat will be gathered into the barn, but the chaff will be burned with a fire that never goes out.
Be careful about your habits.

A recent writer said: “If only young people could see how soon they will become nothing but walking bundles of habits! Then they would pay more attention to how they live while they can still be shaped.
We are spinning our own fate, good or bad, and it can never be undone.
Even the smallest act of goodness or of evil leaves its mark, however tiny.
In Jefferson’s play, the drunkard Rip Van Winkle makes an excuse every time he slips again. He says, ‘I won’t count this time.’
Well, he may not count it, and a kind heaven may not count it. But it is being counted all the same.
Deep down in his nerve cells and fibers, the molecules are counting it. They record it and store it up, to be used against him when the next temptation comes.
Scientifically speaking, nothing we ever do is truly wiped out.
Of course, this has a good side as well as a bad side.

We become lasting drunkards by taking one drink after another. In the same way we become saints in our moral life—and experts in practical and scientific work—by one act after another and one hour of work after another.”
Be careful about temptations. Our Lord taught us to pray, “Do not lead us into temptation.” And again He said, “Watch and pray, so that you do not enter into temptation.”
By nature we are weak and sinful. So it is much better for us to pray to be delivered, rather than to pray for strength to resist once temptation has already caught us.
Prevention is better than cure.
Seeds of passion and evil may be hidden under the soil. They are just waiting for the right moment to spring up.
Young men claim that you have to see both sides of life.
How foolish! I don’t need to put my hand in the fire to see if it will burn.
A steamboat was stuck on the Mississippi River, and the captain could not get it free.
At last a tough-looking man came on board and said:
“Captain, I hear you want a pilot to get you out of this trouble?”
The captain said, “Are you a pilot?”
“Well, that’s what they call me.”
“Do you know where the snags and sandbars are?”
“No, sir.”
“Then how do you expect to get me out of here if you don’t know where the snags and sandbars are?”
“I know where they ain’t!” he answered.
Start sowing good seed while children are young. That way the weeds won’t get a start.
Satan does not wait until they grow up, and neither should we.
Many fishing nets are made so that only full-grown fish are caught. The young ones slip through.
Satan has no nets like that.
He catches the weakest and the youngest.
A young Sunday school teacher said, “We must take care of our boys, or the devil will.”
The old superintendent answered, “The devil will take care of them anyway. The devil will not neglect them, even if we do.”
One of the devil’s cleverest tricks is to make us believe that children cannot understand religion.
Would Christ have made a child the model of faith if He knew that a child could not understand His words?
It is much easier for children to love and trust than it is for adults. So we should set Christ before them as the One they should choose above all else.
Don’t let opportunities slip by.
Napoleon used to say: “In every battle there is a turning point—ten or fifteen minutes—and the outcome of the battle depends on it.
Win that moment and you win; lose it and you are defeated.”
Beware of sin. Its wages are death. And as someone has said, those wages have never been lowered.
Sin fools people. It fools them about how much satisfaction it will give, about the excuses they can make for it, and about how sure the punishment is that must follow.
If sin did not fool us, it would never seem delightful.
It comes looking innocent. Then it drains your lifeblood and takes away your moral strength to do good.
Canon Wilberforce was walking on the Isle of Skye when he saw a magnificent eagle flying upward.
He stopped and watched it fly.
Soon he noticed that something was wrong.
The eagle began to fall, and soon it lay dead at his feet.

He wanted to know why it had died, so he examined it. He found no sign of a gunshot wound. But in its claws he saw a small weasel. During the flight the eagle had pulled the weasel close to its body—and the weasel had sucked the lifeblood from the eagle’s breast.
That is how it ends for everyone who keeps clinging to sin.
Don’t be fooled by how attractive this world is.
It will cheat you and destroy you.
“The Redoubtable” was the name of a French ship. Lord Nelson spared it from destruction twice. Yet it was from the rigging of that very ship that the shot that killed him was fired.
The devil serves many a sin in honey. But there is poison mixed in.
The truest pleasures grow from the good seed of righteousness. No other pleasures are worth anything.
Beware of ignorance and not caring.
You cannot afford to neglect your soul.
There is too much at stake.
I have never known an idle man to be converted.
Until he wakes up and sees how lost and hopeless he is, God Almighty will not reach down and take him by the hand.
Once a ship was in great danger at sea. Everyone but one man was on their knees.
They called to him to come and pray with them, but he answered:
“Not me. Looking after the ship is your job.
I’m only a passenger.”
Remember that just knowing is not enough.
Many people know the teachings and promises of the gospel by heart, but they have not been touched by saving grace.
Knowledge is often useless or even harmful. What we need is to know God’s will and do it.
Even good resolutions are not enough.
No doubt they help in their own way. But the Bible does not lead us to believe that they can save anyone.

It does not say: “To all who resolved to receive Him, He gave the power to become sons of God—to those who resolve to believe in His name.” It says: “To all who received Him * * * who believe in His name.”
Be watchful! We always need to be on guard so that we do not fall into sin.
“Put a double guard on that spot tonight,” a wise officer ordered when an attack was expected.
Even at best there will be some weeds among the wheat.
All of us carry around material that Satan can work with. Paul said:
“I know that nothing good lives in me—that is, in my flesh. I want to do what is good, but I cannot find a way to do it.
I do not do the good I want to do. Instead, I do the evil I do not want to do.
Now if I do what I do not want to do, it is no longer I who am doing it. It is sin living in me.
So I find this law at work: when I want to do good, evil is right there with me.
Deep inside I delight in God’s law. But I see another law at work in my body. It fights against the law of my mind and makes me a prisoner of the law of sin that is in my body.
What a miserable man I am! Who will rescue me from this body of death?”
Praise God, he could add: “I thank God through Jesus Christ our Lord.”
The choice God has put before us is clear: “Whoever believes in the Son has eternal life. Whoever does not believe the Son will not see life, but God’s anger remains on him.”
There is no middle way—“whoever believes”—“whoever does not believe.”
He lets us choose, and the responsibility is ours.
Choosing rightly may cost you many sacrifices and tear at your heart. But I beg you to take that decisive step now.
The salvation of your soul matters more than anything else.
Will you risk your eternity for some gain or pleasure right now?
Bow your head and say: “Heavenly Father, I now choose to come to You as a poor sinner, pleading with You.
I believe in Your Son, whom You sent to be my Savior. I trust in the worth of His blood, which was shed as the sacrifice for my sins. And I rest in the certainty that my sins are forgiven.”
There is hope for the worst sinner.
Wherever weeds grow, good seed can grow too.
The greater your need, the more welcome you will be to Jesus.
He knows the proud and self-confident only from a distance. But even the faintest whisper of a sinner who is truly sorry gets His attention.
Our Lord gave us a simple test to help us choose.
He said, “Every tree is known by its fruit.
A good tree does not produce bad fruit, and a bad tree does not produce good fruit.”
Many of us do not have the time or the ability to untangle complicated arguments or understand deep doctrines.
Some sides of the truth are often hard for ordinary people to grasp.
But the test Christ gave is short and practical. Any one of us can use it.
A missionary asked a Chinese man whom he had not seen at his mission before, “Have you ever heard the gospel?”
“No,” he answered, “but I have seen it.
I know a man who used to be the terror of his neighborhood.
He was a heavy opium smoker and as dangerous as a wild animal. But he was completely changed.
Now he is gentle and good, and he has given up opium.”
Apply this test to unbelief.
What fruit does it produce?
Crime follows wherever it goes.
Society falls apart. Sexual purity, honesty, and the other virtues are undermined.
The whole of life is ruined.
Here is a short passage from a letter written in an English prison. It is a powerful charge against any system of belief that does not acknowledge God:
“I am one of thirteen unbelievers.
Where are my friends?
Four have been hanged.
One became a Christian.
Six have been sentenced to different terms in prison. And one is now locked in a cell right above my head, sentenced to prison for life.”
With all reverence, we can apply this text to our Lord Himself.
He Himself gave us the right to do so.
Once, when the Jews found fault with what He did, He said: “The works the Father has given Me to finish—the very works I am doing—testify about Me that the Father has sent Me.”
Another time they gathered around Him and asked, “How long will You keep us in suspense?
If You are the Christ, tell us plainly.”
Jesus answered: “I told you, and you did not believe.
The works I do in My Father’s name testify about Me. * * * If I do not do My Father’s works, do not believe Me.
But if I do them, even if you do not believe Me, believe the works. Then you will know and believe that the Father is in Me, and I am in Him.”
No wonder Nicodemus, the ruler, said, “Rabbi, we know that You are a teacher who has come from God. No one could do these miracles You do unless God were with him.”

And Peter said: “Men of Israel, listen to these words: Jesus of Nazareth was a man whom God approved among you. God showed this by the miracles, wonders, and signs He did through Jesus among you, as you yourselves know.”
What fruit do wastefulness, pride, and greed produce?
And on the other hand, what fruit do prayer, fearing God, and keeping His commandments produce?
What fruit does heathenism produce?
Look at Africa, China, India, and the islands of the seas, with their gods of wood and stone.
What kind of understanding and moral sense must people have if they will worship such things?
Even the best of the non-Christian religions must always turn out to be a failure.
No one can deny that the writings of heathen philosophers command many of the highest virtues.
How could it be otherwise?
Morality is found wherever there are people. So we can expect that here and there some thinker would see further than most, and understand more deeply the basic truths of right and wrong.
To my mind, this fact only proves how closely the human and the divine are connected.
Christianity never claimed to bring in a brand-new system of morality.
Speaking about another matter, Christ said: “Don’t think that I have come to destroy the law and the prophets. I have not come to destroy, but to fulfill.”
So the fullness and perfection of His own teaching was bound to include many principles that had already appeared in heathen morality.
But in our Savior’s hands they became broader and brighter, and fuller of power and meaning.
Can these non-Christian religions pass the test?
Stoicism was perhaps the noblest of the Greek philosophies. But it quickly turned into complete cynicism. In the end it claimed that no one could ever reach virtue.
Epicureanism started out fairly well. But even before its founder died, it had earned a shameful name: a teaching fit only for pigs.
Look at Buddhism, with its filthy ceremonies and cruel tortures.
All these systems show a conflict between what they teach and what they do.
They failed to reach their goal, because they attacked the problem from the wrong side.
They kept trimming the branch, not seeing that the tree was rotten at its heart.
Only Christianity can pass the test of lifting people out of the pit.
And how does it plan to do that?
Not by making the danger and need seem smaller.
It says: “The whole head is sick, and the whole heart is weak.
From the sole of the foot to the head there is nothing healthy—only wounds and bruises and infected sores.”
The first thing it requires is a new birth—being born again by the Holy Spirit.
“You must be born again.”

It does not put being made holy before being made right with God. First it gives life from above. Then it surrounds the redeemed sinner with the love of Christ and with the fellowship and guidance of the Holy Spirit.
A Chinese man who had become a Christian once said: “I was down in a deep pit, half sunk in the mud, crying for someone to help me out.
When I looked up, I saw a respected old man with gray hair looking down at me.
“‘My son,’ he said, ‘this is a terrible place.’
‘Yes,’ I answered, ‘I fell into it. Can’t you help me out?’
‘My son,’ he replied, ‘I am Confucius.
If you had read my books and done what they taught, you would never have ended up here.’
‘Yes, father,’ I said, ‘but can’t you help me out?’
As I looked, he was gone.
Soon I saw another figure coming. Another man bent over me. This time his eyes were closed and his arms were folded.
He seemed to be looking at some place far away.
‘My son,’ Buddha said, ‘just close your eyes, fold your arms, and forget all about yourself.
Let yourself rest completely.
Don’t think about anything that could disturb you.
Become so still that nothing can move you.
Then, my child, you will enjoy the same sweet rest that I have.’
‘Yes, father,’ I answered, ‘I will when I am above ground.
Can’t you help me out?’
But Buddha was gone too.
I was just starting to give up hope when I saw another figure above me. He was different from the others.
His face showed marks of suffering.
I cried out to Him:
‘Oh, Father! Can You help me?’
‘My child,’ He said, ‘what is wrong?’
Before I could answer, He was down in the mud beside me.
He put His arms around me and lifted me up. Then He fed me and let me rest.
When I was well, He did not say, Now, don’t do that again. Instead He said, ‘We will walk on together now.’ And we have been walking together to this day.”
This was how a poor Chinese man told about the loving compassion and help of the Lord Jesus.
Some time ago I read about a young man who had just come out of a saloon and had gotten on his horse.
A deacon passed by on his way to church. The young man followed him and said,
“Deacon, can you tell me how far it is to hell?”
It hurt the deacon’s heart that a young man like that would talk so carelessly. He kept walking and said nothing.
When he came around the corner to the church, he found that the horse had thrown the young man, and he was dead.
So you may be closer to the Judgment than you think.
When I was in Switzerland many years ago, I learned some serious lessons about how suddenly death can come upon us.
I saw several places where landslides had completely destroyed whole villages. I saw other places where avalanches had swept down the mountainsides and left destruction behind them.
In the year 1806 a terrible disaster struck a village called Goldau. It lay in a fertile valley at the foot of the Rossberg mountain.
The season had been unusually wet, and that had made the crops even more plentiful.
Early one morning a young farmer walked past the cottage of an old man he knew. He saw the old man sitting at his door in the full sunshine.
“Good morning, neighbor,” he said. “It looks like we’ll have a nice day.”
“About time we had a nice day,” the old man grumbled. “It’s been wet enough lately.”
“Have you heard what people are saying?” the young man asked.
“The people who got up earliest this morning say they saw the top of old Rossberg move.”
“Really! That could well be,” said the old man.
“Mark my words—I’ve often said it before. I won’t live to see it. But before the young people of today are as old as I am, the top of that mountain will be lying at its foot.”

“I hope it won’t happen in my lifetime,” said the young man, and he walked on. He had no idea how close the prediction was to coming true. He did not know that the ripening fields of grain and the rich clusters of sweet grapes would never be harvested. But that is how it was.

The heavy rains had overfilled the springs of water inside the mountain. As the water forced its way to the surface and down toward the valley, it loosened huge masses of rounded rock. These rocks were held together by a kind of clay, and the top part of the mountain was made of this material.
At last these huge masses broke loose and crashed down into the valley. They buried the whole village and about eight hundred of its people under their weight.
But what happened to the old man?
Sadly, he did not escape.
He believed the mountain would fall, but he did not think it would happen so soon.
He was sitting in his cottage, calmly smoking his pipe, when the young man came rushing back and shouted:
“The mountain is falling!”
The old man calmly got up from his seat and looked out his door. Then he said:
“I’ll have time to fill my pipe again,” and he went back into his house.
The young man was saved.
The old man died before he had left his cottage. The house and its owner were crushed and swept to the bottom of the valley.
In 1881 I was in the north of England when a terrible storm swept over that part of the country.
A friend of mine was a minister at Eyemouth, and many of the town’s fishermen belonged to his congregation.
The weather had been very stormy, and the fishermen had been stuck in the harbor for a week.
But one day the sun came out in a clear blue sky. It seemed that the storm was over, and the boats headed out to the fishing grounds.
Forty-one boats left the harbor that day.
Before they left, the harbor master raised the storm signal and warned them that a storm was coming.
He begged them not to go. But they ignored his warning, and off they went.
They saw no sign that a storm was coming.
But within a few hours it struck that coast, and very few of those fishermen came back.
There were five or six men in each boat, and almost all of them died in that terrible storm.
In my friend’s church, I believe only three male members were left.
Those men were swept into eternity because they did not listen to the warning.
Now I am raising the storm signal, and I warn you to escape from the judgment that is coming!
Some years ago a man lived near one of the great railroad lines. One night he saw that a landslide had blocked the track.

He looked at the clock and saw that he did not have time to get to the telegraph office to stop the night express. So he grabbed a lantern and ran up the track, hoping to be in time to stop the train.
As he ran, he fell and his light went out.
He had no other match, and he could hear the train coming in the distance.
He didn’t know what to do.
As a last resort he stood on the bank. The moment the train came up beside him, he threw the lantern as hard as he could at the engineer.
The engineer realized that something must be wrong. He heeded the warning, whistled for the brakes, and stopped the train just a few yards from the blockage.
Now I throw the broken lantern at your feet!
I beg you, take warning. Make a clean break with sin, whatever it costs.
Take warning! You must either give up sin, or give up the hope of heaven.
Put yourself where you can be blessed.
Make up your mind now that by God’s grace you will win the victory.
“Let the wicked give up his way, and the evil man his thoughts. Let him return to the Lord, and He will have mercy on him. Let him return to our God, for He will forgive freely and fully.”
